HERE-SBD EV Index 2026 Reveals That a Quarter of EV Owners Consider a Hybrid for Their Next Car
65 photos
Photo: Toyota
Per a study made possible by Here Technologies and SBD Automotive, more battery-electric vehicle owners want a hybrid or a more heavily electrified internal combustion model as their next car. The share favoring hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and extended-range electric vehicles increased from 23 percent in 2025 to 28 percent this year, and that increase speaks volumes about consumer preferences.
While it may not mean that electric vehicle owners have suddenly fallen out of love with their Teslas, the HERE-SBD EV Index 2026 found that more than a third are really considering hybridized vehicles. At the same time, 64 percent of surveyed BEV owners remain likely to purchase another fully electric model.
Those numbers can easily coexist. Think about it this way: someone might appreciate the smooth acceleration, lower running costs, and quiet operation of a BEV while questioning whether the battery-only powertrain suits every journey they make. In other words, even BEV owners understand that battery-electric vehicles have their downsides.
Here and SBD surveyed more than 4,000 drivers across the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Spain, India, and Australia, with the researchers examining a bunch of data. Such data includes ownership experiences, purchasing intentions, the charging infrastructure, and the factors that influence the BEV owner's next vehicle decision.
SBD Automotive's Robert Fisher argues that manufacturers need to understand why existing BEV customers still consider alternatives. Put it this way: a plug-in hybrid is the better pick for longer trips because of its combustion engine. Plugging into a charging station and planning the trip with charging stops in mind is not necessary in this case, and the same can be said about EREVs.
While the EREV may seem pretty similar to the PHEV, bear in mind that extended-range electric vehicles never use their combustion engines to drive the wheels directly. The combustion engine in an EREV is there only to generate electricity, which is fed to either the drive units or the high-voltage battery.
Photo: Toyota The EREV and PHEV, therefore, offer a different compromise between electric driving and the convenience of dinosaur juice. Looking at the bigger picture, the household situation also matters. The HERE-SBD EV Index 2026 found that 65 percent of surveyed BEV owners replaced their only vehicle with an electric model, effectively becoming electric-only households.
Such households rely on public charging networks on longer trips, and a broken charger is more than just a minor inconvenience if you are planning to drive 600 miles in a single day. A broken charger forces the driver to change plans, finding another charging location with fewer than 100 miles of range displayed by their car. I, for one, really hate those situations with a passion.
Something else I can't stand is how every single charging network where I live wants you to install their dedicated apps, forcing me to input my card details time and time again. And boy, I sure feel impatient when there's a line of battery-electric vehicles in front of me at the charging location of my liking. In many respects, I'm still identifying with team internal combustion, be it electrified or not.
Interestingly enough, the HERE-SBD EV Index 2026 indicates that 68 percent of BEV owners are pleased with the charging situation. 67 percent, meanwhile, are pleased with their vehicle's driving range. From the standpoint of hybrid consideration, Italy leads the way, with 39 percent of BEV owners considering a hybrid as their next vehicle.
The US, UK, and Germany have much stronger BEV loyalty. The motivations behind BEV purchases have also changed, with better value for money ranking first among respondents. Lower running costs followed suit at 34 percent, while environmental benefits came third at 33 percent.
Among owners of internal combustion vehicles, only 17 percent identified electric models for their next purchase or lease.
Via // SBD Automotive

Sinking of the SS United States Pushed a Day Earlier, Goodbye Ceremony Cancelled
10 photos
Photo: Okaloosa Board of County Commissioners/Facebook
The official ending of SS United States isn’t a quiet one. After the Okaloosa Board of County Commissioners’ official announcement in late October that the iconic ship would be sunk Thursday, on November 12, first a last-effort legal battle tried to halt the process altogether, then weather predictions brought another bump in the road. The date has now officially changed to Wednesday, November 11, but the planned farewell ceremony is definitively cancelled.
The sinking of the SS United States is one of the saddest events this year for historic ship aficionados in the US. Even if Okaloosa officials have tried to paint this as a happy event, given that the ship will become what is considered to be the largest artificial reef in the world, sure to attract lots of divers and tourists to Destin, Florida, everyone can feel the heaviness of this historic event that feels tragic.
A comment on the Okaloosa Board’s official Facebook page stated that “Even in death, she looks more powerful than ships today,” and another echoed that sentiment by adding that “There will never be another beautiful lady such as this”, yet people are still debating on whether this was the right decision for SS United States.
The “preservationist” side believes that the iconic ocean liner should have been saved, refitted, and turned into an active commercial ship, or at least a museum. On the other side, officials have argued that the ship was beyond repair and that trying to hold on to it would be far too costly; instead, sinking it in order to become a man-made reef would provide benefits for the marine environment and for the community, while still preserving the ship’s memory.
Last Monday, the SS United States Preservation Foundation, a small non-profit that was very active in trying to save the ship from reefing, filed a law suit trying to stop the process, and a motion seeking a temporary restraining order. The law suit argued that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers hadn’t properly addressed the potential environmental impact, and historic preservation concerns were also added.
However, the final decision of a Florida federal judge denied these requests, allowing Okaloosa officials to move forward with the planned sinking. That’s when, unexpectedly, weather conditions caused another turn of events. A controlled sinking is much more complex than it sounds, and highly weather-dependent.
According to Okaloosa County, because “unsafe weather conditions” are forecast for Thursday, the controlled sinking was moved a day earlier, which also happens to be Veterans Day, an added symbolism that many people seemed to appreciate. For the same reason, the sendoff ceremony that was supposed to take place a day before the sinking, was also cancelled.
Folks everywhere will still be able to watch the sinking live-streamed – the link for it will be shared officially on thessus.com, prior to the event. Yesterday, the ship has officially left Mobile, Alabama, headed toward Destin, Florida. The deployment is set to begin at 1 p.m. CST.
If no new obstacle shows up, the American ocean liner that broke the record as the fastest passenger ship to cross the Atlantic will be sunk forever , and turned into the world’s largest artificial reef.

source_document.body:
Cold storage facility operator Lineage said customer inventories have stabilized, though some accounts are holding lower stock levels. The Novi, Michigan-based company said Tuesday on its third-quarter call that it continues to shutter underutilized facilities in efforts to tighten supply and reduce debt leverage.
Lineage ( NASDAQ: LINE ) noted that it and Americold ( NYSE: COLD ), the top two operators in the space, have reduced overall capacity by 4% (9 million square feet) over the past two years. Lineage has idled 16 locations since the start of 2025, representing 2.6 million square feet and 212,000 pallet positions.
The company reported a third-quarter net loss of $173 million, or 68 cents per share. Adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) were 73 cents per share, down 12 cents year over year. (AFFO excludes depreciation, acquisition costs, restructuring expenses and other non-recurring items.)
Consolidated net revenue of $1.36 billion was down 1% y/y and just shy of the $1.37-billion consensus estimate.
An 8% y/y decline in food-related container volumes dragged revenue lower. The company pointed to weakness in the seafood sector as higher fuel costs forced fishermen to curtail their trips. Elevated diesel prices also pushed Lineage’s third-party transportation costs higher in the quarter.
However, facility occupancy is improving across the portfolio.
Table: Lineage’s key performance indicators
On a same-warehouse comparison, Lineage’s physical occupancy was 76.2% in the quarter, 110 basis points higher y/y, and 40 bps better than the second quarter . (Physical occupancy was 76.4% in the first quarter .)
Pallet throughput declined 1% y/y, with storage revenue per pallet down 2%. Both metrics were up less than 1% sequentially.
“Our core business trends continued to stabilize in the third quarter, with same-store occupancy growing year-over-year for the second consecutive quarter, further confirmation that customer inventory levels have normalized,” said Lineage President and CEO Greg Lehmkuhl in a news release.
Adjusted EBITDA of $317 million was 7% lower y/y, with the adjusted EBITDA margin falling 150 bps to 23.3%.
The company lowered its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance by 1% at the midpoint of the new range of $1.25 billion to $1.27 billion. A fire at a California facility is expected to be a $20-million headwind. (Lineage reported $1.3 billion in adjusted EBITDA in 2025.)
The AFFO guidance range was tightened to $2.86 to $2.98 per share.
It has 17 facilities currently under construction, which will add $141 million in net operating income, $11 million of which has already been achieved.
Lineage ended the third quarter with net debt at 6.4 times last 12 months’ adjusted EBITDA. It said that proceeds from asset dispositions and insurance recoveries should lower its leverage to a target range of 5 to 5.5x, with meaningful progress occurring in the 2027 first half.
Lineage manages 497 facilities with 3.1 billion cubic feet of space across North America, Europe and the Asia-Pacific region. It also provides freight forwarding, customs brokerage, drayage and truck transportation.
Shares of LINE were down 9.6% in early trading on Tuesday compared to the S&P 500, which was off 0.6%.
Why it matters? Lineage is one of only two publicly traded cold storage providers. Its quarterly results provide a look at macro trends across the temperature-controlled warehousing and transportation markets.

source_document.body:
SONAR’s new MCP connector lets compatible AI assistants like Claude and Copilot answer freight market questions in plain language, drawing on SONAR data and tools for rates, capacity, lanes, carrier safety and more.
SONAR has launched SONAR MCP, a connector that puts its freight market intelligence directly inside compatible AI assistants like Claude, Copilot and more. The rollout to SONAR customers began the week of Nov. 9, 2026.
Instead of moving between dashboards and memorizing index tickers, transportation teams can now ask a question in plain English and get an answer grounded in SONAR data.
What is SONAR MCP?
SONAR MCP is SONAR’s connector built on the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets AI models and agents connect to outside tools and data. Anthropic introduced the protocol in November 2024, and it works much like an API built for AI.
Once the SONAR connector is turned on, a user’s AI assistant decides which SONAR tools to call based on the question asked and the user’s SONAR permissions. It then combines the results into a single plain-language answer.
What freight data can AI assistants access through SONAR MCP?
SONAR MCP provides 24 tools spanning six areas of freight intelligence:
Spot and contract rates, including SAMA rate projections
Market conditions, such as tender rejections, volumes and capacity
Lane intelligence, including how difficult a lane is to cover
SONAR index data
Ocean freight metrics, including container bookings
FMCSA carrier safety and inspection statistics
According to SONAR, anything available through its API is also available through MCP, across truckload, intermodal , LTL and ocean.
How does SONAR MCP work? A live example from F3
SONAR demonstrated the connector live at F3 this year, using Claude as the AI assistant. The presenter asked a common shipper question: if a company moves 500 truckloads a year from Los Angeles to Chicago, could it save money by switching to intermodal?
The AI assistant pulled SONAR’s truckload and intermodal rate data for the lane, compared the two modes and answered in plain language: switching to intermodal would save money.
The demo then walked through a holiday inventory scenario moving from China through the Port of Los Angeles. In one conversation, the assistant checked ocean bookings from China to Los Angeles, Chicago intermodal volume, LTL pricing and outbound truckload capacity in Los Angeles.
Asked to summarize the risk before a budget meeting, the assistant flagged Chicago to Louisville as the most exposed lane. It suggested locking in contract rates there before the holiday season.
See the rates and market conditions SONAR MCP returned in the full F3 demo .
Who is SONAR MCP for?
SONAR MCP is built for shippers, freight brokers, 3PLs, carriers and analysts who make decisions with freight market data. The F3 demo showed just a peak into the many ways each group can use it. SONAR will also be rolling out guidance on additional use cases.
Shippers preparing bids: a messy, eight-tab bid file went into the AI assistant and came back as a clean lane list with SONAR rate benchmarks, lane scores and call-outs, such as a 4 a.m. pickup that may add cost.
Brokers reporting to leadership: an export of 60 loads from a TMS became a one-page PDF comparing the brokerage’s performance with SONAR benchmarks.
Teams building their own tools: a SONAR shipper expert built a forward-looking network risk forecaster with an AI assistant. It refreshes with live SONAR data every day through MCP, with no software team or API project required.
SONAR groups the use cases into five areas: market intelligence, pricing and procurement, capacity and risk, research and reporting, and network and lane analysis.
Why SONAR MCP matters for freight teams
SONAR MCP lowers the barrier to using freight data. Users no longer need to know which dashboard holds an answer or which ticker to type.
During the F3 demo, the presenter noted that LTL pricing data in SONAR normally requires a specific ticker. Through MCP, a plain question returned the same answer.
The launch also responds directly to customer feedback about the sheer volume of data in SONAR.
“SONAR MCP puts the full depth of SONAR data right in front of our users, inside the AI platform they already choose to work in,” said Julie Van de Kamp, chief commercial officer at SONAR. “We’ve heard from customers that SONAR can feel hard to use or that the data is overwhelming. MCP removes that barrier. Ask a question in plain language, and your AI assistant pulls the SONAR data and summarizes the key findings for you.”
What’s next for SONAR and AI?
SONAR said at F3 that it is developing AI agents native to the SONAR platform, which would add more market context to answers. The company expects to share more in early 2027.
How to get started with SONAR MCP
SONAR MCP is rolling out to SONAR customers now, and the tools available depend on each user’s SONAR permissions. To learn more, visit gosonar.com , read the SONAR MCP overview or contact set up a demo . For background on SONAR’s data, see the freight market intelligence guide .

An aerial view of the Madison project in Montana. Photo Credit: American Pacific Mining
By: Northern Miner Staff November 10, 2026
A gold-copper intercept below old workings in Montana and a U.S. defence award for nickel exploration in Michigan show two ways early-stage projects can advance. In Nevada, explorers are testing whether a phosphate bed holds together along strike and whether old silver and base-metal workings conceal a larger sulphide system. Here are four projects to watch before they reach a resource estimate.
American Pacific Mining
American Pacific Mining (CSE: USGD; US-OTC: USGDF) is testing for a larger gold-copper system beneath the historical workings at its Madison project, about 40 km southeast of Butte, Mont. A 15,000-metre drill program is testing both shallow skarn and vein targets and deeper porphyry-style mineralization that could be their source.
Drill hole M26C-02 cut 30.8 metres grading 7.4 grams gold per tonne, 9.6 grams silver and 0.29% copper from 218.2 metres depth, American Pacific reported in September . That included 20.1 metres at 11.15 grams gold, 14.3 grams silver and 0.42% copper. The massive sulphide mineralization remains open and appears to thicken to the southwest, the company said.
The drill hole tested the ground between the historical Madison and Broadway workings, where the company is looking for a connection between previously identified high-grade zones. In October, American Pacific said it planned geophysical and structural surveys in the drill hole to guide step-out drilling.
Madison produced copper and gold intermittently from underground workings. Rio Tinto (ASX, LSE, NYSE: RIO) subsidiary Kennecott Exploration spent several years exploring the property under an earn-in agreement before returning it to American Pacific. The junior also holds the Ziggurat gold and Gooseberry silver-gold projects in Nevada.
American Pacific Mining had a market value of about C$41.4 million at print time.
Bitterroot Resources
Bitterroot Resources (TSXV: BTT) is preparing to drill its LM nickel-copper project in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula after securing U.S. government backing to look for a domestic source of high-grade nickel.
The U.S. Department of Defense agreed in September to provide up to $5.22 million (C$7.4 million) under the Defense Production Act, Bitterroot said. The award is expected to cover half of approved exploration spending, including drilling, surveys and permitting. The company arranged a C$2.4-million private placement to help fund its share and provide working capital.
Bitterroot planned to start 15 to 20 drill holes in the fourth quarter, each 500 to 700 metres long, to locate the bedrock source of high-grade nickel-copper sulphides. Earlier drilling totalled 7,565 metres in 26 core holes and identified a magma conduit with nickel-copper and platinum group metal sulphides in 10 of them.
Bitterroot subsidiary Trans Superior Resources operates LM and owns 51%. Private Michigan explorer Below Exploration holds the balance. The project sits in the Baraga Basin, in the same peninsula as Talon Metals’ (TSX: TLO; US-OTC: TLOFF) Eagle nickel mine.
Bitterroot Resources had a market value of about C$18 million at print time.
Nevada Organic Phosphate
Nevada Organic Phosphate (CSE: NOP; US-OTC: NOPFF) is tracing a shallow phosphate bed at Murdock Mountain in northeastern Nevada as it looks for a potential domestic source of fertilizer feedstock.
Murdock Mountain in northeastern Nevada is a potential domestic source of fertilizer feedstock. Credit: Nevada Organic Phosphate
A 1.5-km step-out extended confirmed mineralization along the upper phosphate zone to more than 3 km of strike, the company reported in August. Drill hole MM26-10 returned 3.6 metres averaging 10.89% phosphorus pentoxide. The company brought a drill contractor back in September to continue testing the trend.
The company interprets the phosphate as a nearly flat-lying sedimentary bed in the Phosphoria Formation, which hosts deposits across parts of the western U.S. It is assessing whether the rock could qualify for organic fertilizer use, citing low concentrations of heavy metals, uranium and thorium.
Murdock Mountain lies near Montello, about 665 km north of Las Vegas and 6 km from a railway. Drilling is aimed at establishing the bed’s continuity, thickness and grade ahead of any resource or economic study.
Nevada Organic Phosphate had a market value of about C$23 million at print time.
North Peak Resources
North Peak Resources (TSXV: NPR; US-OTC: NPRLF) has added diamond drilling at Prospect Mountain near Eureka, Nev., to test for sulphides beneath and around historical workings.
The company began reverse-circulation drilling in August and added a diamond rig in September after reviewing geophysical survey results. The roughly 7,000-metre program targets five areas. Initial diamond drilling is focused on the main sulphide anomaly, with deeper holes testing conductive targets that could represent extensions of the mineralization.
Earlier drilling found narrow intervals of high-grade zinc and silver in massive sulphides. The new program tests whether those intervals connect to a larger system at depth. North Peak secured an on-site water supply over the summer, clearing a practical hurdle to deeper drilling.
Prospect Mountain lies at the southern end of the Battle Mountain–Eureka trend. Historical mining targeted shallow gold, silver and base-metal mineralization, while deeper targets have seen relatively little modern exploration.
North Peak Resources had a market value of about C$36 million at print time. Print

By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
10 November 2026
When it rains, it pours. Agriculture exporters in Latin America’s southern cone have struggled with headwinds from weather hitting crops as well as transport routes, on top of gateway problems and high transport costs.
Chile’s cherry export season got off to a rocky start when truckers staged a protest about high costs that cut off access to the container terminals at the port of San Antonio. They were up in arms over stalled freight rates, rising fuel costs and new charges on the main highway between the port and Santiago.
The strike disrupted the official start of Chile’s cherry export season that was set to kick off with the sailing of the first ‘Cherry Express’ to China, scheduled for 9 November, with loading planned to commence two days earlier.
San Antonio is the nation’s main gateway for marine cherry exports, which have gained ground over airfreight in recent years. The port reportedly handles nearly half of Chile’s fruit exports.
Industry body Frutas de Chile called for a swift end to the strike, warning that a prolonged stand-off would affect crop quality, as the port was already at 90% of storage capacity.
The blockade was called off late on Friday after nine days, following an agreement on an 8% adjustment on overland freight rates and a commitment to implement an indexing mechanism. By that time, however, the first ‘Cherry Express’ had been diverted to Valparaiso, causing a scramble to move cherries there.
For growers, the disruption piled additional grief on a reduced crop of inferior quality as a result of massive rainfall caused by this year’s El Niño, which has been flagged as an extreme weather event and affected crops in other parts of South America as well.
“Exporters in Chile have been very worried about the situation,” reported Federico Calvo, director of Intermodal Logistics. “Cherry volumes are starting up, but not as strong.”
On 2 November, Chile’s Ministry of Agriculture declared an agricultural emergency in parts of the Maule region, an area dominated by forestry and agriculture, especially wine growing. Media reported serious damage caused by rains, hailstorms and strong winds.
El Niño also hit Argentine exporters. Snow on the Andean passes and heavy rain repeatedly blocked the main road from Argentina to the Chilean ports, resulting in ten days of closures at the border.
Typically, border crossings are closed during the southern winter only for a couple of days, Mr Calvo said.
The situation is causing concern for blueberry growers in Argentina and Chile, just as they are poised to benefit from a weather-related slowdown of blueberry exports from Peru. Their northern rivals had thundered to the top of South America’s blueberry-producing nations with a rapid expansion of cultivated areas.
This year, El Niño has impacted Peruvian blueberry output, opening the door to growers in the south to boost their exports. Proarandanos, the Peruvian blueberry industry body, has lowered its forecast for this year’s crop several times. Its most recent forecast, from mid-October, is 6% lower than the projection from the beginning of that month, and down 10% year on year, despite a 15% increase in the acreage for production. Predictions for the fourth quarter flag a decline of nearly 25%.
Last week, Peru’s Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism called a meeting with government agencies and industry bodies to discuss measures to maintain operations during climate-related disruptions. Among the proposals that came up at the event are identifying vulnerable ports and transport routes, evaluating alternative routes and setting up response procedures for logistics disruptions.
Chilean and Argentine shippers using or contemplating airfreight to move produce to overseas markets have also faced challenges. The current upgrading of the secondary runway at Buenos Aires’ Ezeiza airport involves work on the intersection with the airport’s main runway from 26 October to 15 November, which cut the latter’s length from 3,300m to 1,850m. Several airlines have suspended flights to Ezeiza for the period, while a few have added refuelling stops in Montevideo or Sao Paulo to reduce take-off weight at Ezeiza. As a result, airfreight pricing has gone up, Mr Calvo noted.
He added that fuel surcharge adjustments of several airlines serving the Chilean capital have translated into price increases up to 35% there, which have also been hard to stomach for produce shippers.

How much trucking capacity is on the road right now depends almost entirely on which carriers you are counting, because the national fleet is really several different markets stacked together, the owner-operators running a truck or two, the mid-sized fleets, and the largest carriers, and each of those groups is in a different place heading into year-end, which is why a single top-line number tends to hide more than it shows. Break the tractor counts out by fleet size and the gaps between those segments become the real capacity story.
The Top-Line Signals Are Mixed
Before going tier by tier, it helps to set the backdrop, and the backdrop is not sending one clean signal. The SONAR Truckload Rejection Index, which tracks how often carriers turn down the freight shippers tender to them, sits at 12.95 percent. That is above its trailing 12-month average of 8.18 percent, so capacity is tighter than it was a year ago, but it has also eased down from the mid-teens readings it hit over the summer, so the tightening has lost some momentum rather than accelerating.
Volume tells a similarly flat story. The SONAR Truckload Volume Index, a measure of accepted electronic tender volume, sits at 11,636.92, essentially flat on the day and only marginally above its 12-month average of 11,489.59. Freight is moving at a steady clip, neither falling off nor breaking out. Put those two together and the national picture is a standoff, demand holding, capacity a little tighter than last year but no longer tightening hard. That is exactly why the more useful read right now is underneath the top line, in how capacity is distributed by fleet size.
Tractors run by the smallest fleets of one to six power units peaked near 398,000 in early 2023 and have declined steadily to 362,033, giving back the entire pandemic-era surge over three and a half years. Source: FreightWaves SONAR (TCTCO.USA).
The Owner-Operator Segment Has Round-Tripped Its Boom
Start with the smallest carriers, because they have moved the most. SONAR’s count of tractors run by fleets with one to six power units stands at 362,033, and the five-year view is the one that matters. This segment sat near 362,000 tractors in early 2022, surged to a peak close to 398,000 in the first half of 2023 as pandemic-era freight and easy authority pulled a wave of new entrants into the market, and has declined almost without interruption ever since. It is now back to roughly where it started, below its five-year average of about 378,800 and below its 12-month average of about 364,960.
That is close to 36,000 tractors, on the order of nine percent of the segment, pulled back out of the most fragile tier of the market over three and a half years. These are the operators most exposed to the spot market , with the least cost advantage on fuel, insurance, and maintenance, and the thinnest cushion to ride out weak rates, so when conditions soften they are the first to park a truck or let an authority lapse. The entire pandemic-era surge in small-carrier capacity has effectively been unwound, which is a very different starting point than the market had a couple of years ago, whichever way demand breaks from here.
Tractors run by mid-sized fleets of 20 to 100 power units have climbed steadily to a record 470,402, the only fleet-size tier still growing. Source: FreightWaves SONAR (TCTCM.USA).
The Mid-Market Is Setting Records
The mid-sized fleet is the counterweight. SONAR’s count of tractors run by carriers with 20 to 100 power units sits at 470,402, a fresh high, up about a half percent in its latest monthly reading and comfortably above its trailing 12-month average of roughly 451,600. Over five years this band has climbed steadily from about 420,000 tractors to this new record, and unlike the other two tiers it has barely paused.
This is the segment built to absorb. These carriers are big enough to hold real contract freight, run drop-and-hook programs, and operate the lease-on fleets that owner-operators sign onto when running their own authority stops penciling out. When a driver gives up a one-truck operation and leases onto a larger carrier, that tractor does not leave the road, it moves from being counted in the one-to-six tier into a mid-sized fleet. Part of what the record in this band likely reflects is that migration, capacity shifting from the bottom of the market into its middle rather than exiting the industry altogether. One caveat belongs here, because these counts are built from carriers’ MCS-150 filings, so some of the apparent movement into the 20-to-100 band can be carriers updating their paperwork rather than trucks physically changing fleets, which is a reason to read the multi-year trend rather than lean on any single month.
Tractors run by the largest fleets of 1,000-plus power units fell 2.23 percent in the latest reading to 440,430, below their 12-month average, as the biggest carriers hold capacity lean. Source: FreightWaves SONAR (TCTCE.USA).
The Biggest Fleets Are Running Lean
The largest carriers round out the picture, and they are not expanding. SONAR’s count of tractors run by fleets with 1,000 or more power units sits at 440,430, down a sharp 2.23 percent in its latest monthly reading, a drop of more than 10,000 tractors, leaving it below its trailing 12-month average of about 452,800. The five-year line for this group is the choppiest of the three, swinging from near 485,000 tractors in early 2022 down into the 430,000s, back toward 475,000 in late 2024, then grinding lower through 2025 and 2026 with a sharp dip toward 418,000 over the summer before a partial bounce.
The behavior here looks like discipline. The largest fleets can right-size faster than anyone, declining to renew leases, parking underutilized tractors, and trimming fleets that are not earning within a quarter, and the volatility in this line is the fingerprint of exactly that. For now they are holding their counts lean and below their own average, which means the tier most capable of adding a lot of capacity quickly is choosing not to.
Both Ends Are Thin, The Middle Is Full
Line the three tiers up and a clear shape appears. The smallest one-to-six band has round-tripped its boom and sits below its averages. The largest 1,000-plus band is running lean and below its average. Only the mid-sized 20-to-100 band is at a record. Capacity is concentrating in the middle of the market, pulled up from the bottom by owner-operators who lease on or fold, and kept in check at the top by giants who are not re-expanding.
What that might signal is worth thinking through carefully rather than forcing into a forecast. On one hand, the capacity base at the bottom is structurally thinner than it has been in years, and thin, exited small-carrier capacity does not come back on a dime, so if freight demand firms, the market could tighten faster than the flat rejection reading suggests today. On the other hand, with rejections already easing off their summer highs and volumes holding flat, there is no demand pull right now forcing that to happen. The honest read is a loaded-but-quiet setup, a capacity base that has quietly thinned at both ends while the top-line waits for a catalyst. That is a lens on the months ahead, not a prediction of them.
Net changes in trucking authorities swung to a positive 1,279 in the latest reading, well above the 12-month average near 335, though recent figures are distorted by the FMCSA Motus rollout, which paused some deactivations while pushing a backlog of reinstatements through. Source: FreightWaves SONAR (CDNCA.USA).
The Churn Beneath The Net Numbers
The net figures sit on top of constant churn in the federal authority rolls. In a single day’s file of FMCSA Motus carrier changes dated November 9, there were 367 operating-authority updates across 362 individual carriers, of which 199 were in active status, 103 were inactive, 57 were pending, and 8 were formally withdrawn, and more than 90 percent were motor carriers of property carrying the familiar 750,000 dollar insurance requirement. That file comes with a real caveat right now, because the Motus system rollout has paused certain USDOT deactivations tied to biannual update requirements while pushing a backlog of reinstatements through at the same time, which distorts the active and inactive tallies and makes any single day a poor read on true entry and exit. It is a reminder that the authority rolls are in constant motion rather than a clean count of who is coming and going, and because the file carries no fleet-size information, it cannot on its own say which size of carrier is lapsing. The fleet-size picture has to come from the SONAR tractor counts above, not from the authority file.
The Takeaway For The Small Carrier
For the owner-operator reading their own segment in that long decline, the point is not that the small carrier is finished, it is to understand what the last three and a half years selected for. The operators still standing are the ones who know their true cost per mile, who built direct relationships with local shippers instead of living and dying by spot postings, and who ran the business like a business rather than a truck payment. In a market that is tighter than last year but not yet pulling hard in anyone’s favor, that structure is what separates the carriers positioned to benefit if the market firms from the ones who keep showing up in the inactive column no matter what rates do.
Why It Matters
Capacity is not a single number that is cleanly rising or falling right now, it is splitting by fleet size, with the smallest operators having unwound their entire pandemic boom, the largest carriers running deliberately lean, and the mid-sized fleets at a record as they absorb what the bottom lets go. For carriers, brokers, and shippers, the value in that split is as a current lens rather than a forecast, because it shows a capacity base that has quietly thinned at both ends while demand holds flat, and that is the kind of setup that decides how fast the market can move whenever the next real catalyst, up or down, finally arrives.
This analysis draws on FreightWaves SONAR data as of early November 2026: tractor counts by fleet size for the 1-to-6 power-unit segment (TCTCO.USA) at 362,033, the 20-to-100 segment (TCTCM.USA) at 470,402, and the 1,000-plus segment (TCTCE.USA) at 440,430, the SONAR Truckload Rejection Index ( STRI.USA ) at 12.95 percent, and the SONAR Truckload Volume Index (STVI.USA) at 11,636.92.

Delicious 1972 Airstream Argosy Is the Cutest Retro Home Tiny Home You'll See This Week
16 photos
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings
The retro look won't work for everyone, but that's ok: we're all different, and as such, we're probably destined not to like the same things. That said, even someone who is passionately against the sugary retro style will probably appreciate the appeal of this Airstream Argosy turned into a tiny home.
The original rounded series of Argosy travel trailers was in production for about 8 years, between 1972 and 1980, but the exact number of produced units remains a mystery. They're now Airstream unicorns, but back in the day, Airstream regarded them more like the poor and simple cousin from out of town that you're ashamed to be seen in public with.
Brochures referred to them as "the almost Airstream" or the entry-level Airstream: a travel trailer that looked like an Airstream and was supposedly built with the same attention to quality work and quality materials as an Airstream, but that was not , in fact, an Airstream .
An Argosy was cheaper because it was usually built with discarded materials from the main Airstream factory. It was assembled at another facility and did not get you into the Airstream clubs and owners community, though dealers would still service it.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings An Argosy was painted, which the "real" Airstream, with its iconic silver bullet sheen of polished, riveted aluminum, never was. An Argosy was, in short, the lesser Airstream: an Airstream by birth but not one by education and, as such, never quite welcome at the Airstream family table.
Times have changed.
With them, so has the RV community attitude to the Argosy, the painted aluminum, to the point where today they're icons that become coveted collectibles . They change hands for high prices as well, as you'd expect from a collectible, even if they're no longer able to travel the country as they were once meant to do.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings This is the case with the unit we're looking at today, a 1972 Argosy turned into a tiny house. Any Airstream, whether Argosy or not, was imagined as a sort of tiny house on wheels, if only on account of the fact that it comes with all the creature comforts and space for the entire family.
This one still has wheels but most likely won't be using them. It's being sold out of South Carolina as a fixed guest house slash rental slash permanent home for a couple, with a completely redone interior and accessories that are optional but necessary. It's still an Argosy, and a gorgeous one at it, but it's also different.
The biggest change to the original layout of the 22-footer (6.7 meters) is the removal of the onboard bathroom to create a larger footprint and more moving space. Instead, the current owner added a separate bathhouse with a spacious shower, a nice vanity with storage, and what looks like a plumbed toilet.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings With the bathhouse, the listing also mentions the possibility of getting the deck at an extra price. It would make sense for the future owner to choose the bundle, since they're all styled to match.
The Argosy, described as one of the first to roll off the production line (not that this is truly relevant), retains the two-tone paintjob the old models had – this one in striking turquoise and white. Inside, you get all-plywood walls and ceiling, with refurbished floors and wood-trimmed windows.
You also get colorful furniture in shades that match whatever retro expectations you set when you first saw the exterior. Turquoise cabinets, bright yellow sleeping areas, white and turquoise tiled counters, and bright green trimming to add an even more striking pop of color. It's all very retro but also sweet, delicious, and cozy.
Photo: Elise/Tiny House Listings The listing mentions a queen bed in the rear bedroom space, with a smart TV mounted on a wall and a large storage compartment underneath. A large arch to the entrance of the bedroom creates some sense of separation, though not actual privacy for whoever is sleeping inside.
At the other end of the trailer, in what functions as the living room, is a sofa in bright yellow. It's a sleeper sofa, so you can probably accommodate one or two overnight guests in case of an emergency, assuming they don't mind the absence of an indoor bathroom and the aforementioned lack of privacy.

2010 Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss Emerges From Hiding, Has 32.9 Miles on the Clock
30 photos
Photo: RM Sotheby's
The final 2010 Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss ever built has just come out of its hiding place to look for a new home. The ultra-exclusive, ultra-rare automobile is expected to fetch in excess of $6 million.
This Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss was completed on December 22, 2009, as a 2010 model. It is number 75 of 75 units ever built as a tribute to Sir Stirling Moss’s career and his 1955 Mille Miglia victory. That run is considered one of the greatest drives in motor racing history.
With co-driver Denis Jenkinson in the passenger seat and driving a Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR , sporting the iconic racing number 722 (which designated their starting time of 7:22 AM), Moss, then 25, set an all-time speed record that was never broken before the race was permanently discontinued.
Moss completed the grueling, non-stop 992-mile loop on open public roads across Italy, starting and finishing in Brescia, northern Italy, in 10 hours, 7 minutes, and 48 seconds, averaging a staggering 97.96 mph (157.65 kph) and finishing with a massive 32-minute lead over Juan Manuel Fangio.
Photo: RM Sotheby's That is exactly what the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss honors. This final car of the series was commissioned by a member of the Kuwait Royal Family and features a completely bespoke specification, which sets it apart from the standard Crystal Laurite Silver models that dominated the 75-unit production run and positions it as a holy grail for collectors.
Car number 75 left the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC) in Woking, Surrey, England, bound for Switzerland as a closing chapter of the historic Mercedes-Benz and McLaren partnership, codenamed "Project 7." It was first registered on March 10, 2010. Later on, in 2024, it entered a private collection in the United States.
Finished in an exclusive Fire Opal Red, paint code 000U, instead of the standard silver, the car comes with a Silver Arrow red-leather interior with contrasting bespoke yellow stitching, wrapping custom wide, oversized seats in red and black leather.
Unlike the standard production McLaren Stirling Moss examples that used exposed carbon fiber, this example features unique, highly advanced composite material, Alutex aluminum, giving the cabin a bright, gleaming, metallic silver finish.
Photo: RM Sotheby's It is also one of only two McLaren Stirling Moss examples in existence to feature an audio system. The other one, finished in Rosso Corsa, belongs to the Royal Family of Jordan, because money can buy anything, even in a car designed without one.
The standard model was built as a hyper-minimalist, hardcore track speedster and was delivered from the factory completely stripped of creature comforts. There was no infotainment screen, no telephone connectivity, no navigation, and absolutely no radio or sound system.
Mercedes-Benz engineered it that way to maximize weight savings, and because the open cockpit design does not involve a roof, side windows, or a windshield , wind noise at speed is so violent that a conventional car radio would be basically unhearable.
There are, however, two tiny glass wind deflectors, designed to divert air over the cabin, but at high speed, they become pretty much useless. And speaking of speed, the Mercedes-Benz SLR McLaren Stirling Moss is powered by the 5.4-liter supercharged AMG V8, which pumps out 641 horsepower (650 metric horsepower) and 605 pound-feet (820 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: RM Sotheby's That is what makes it flash from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 3.4 seconds and all the way to a top speed of 220 mph (354 kph), aerodynamically limited due to the open-cockpit configuration. A five-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels.
High-performance Brembo carbon-ceramic brakes, assisted by a rear spoiler that acts as a 65-degree active airbrake, provide the stopping power. Exclusively on this final Chassis 75, the multi-piston brake calipers are finished in gold from the factory.
However, the owner did not enjoy all that performance much. The odometer of the car shows just 32.9 miles (53 kilometers), which is basically delivery mileage plus driving up and down the ramp of a trailer for maintenance over all these years.
The model was homologated and road-registered for the United States. It is actually believed to be the only SLR Stirling Moss in existence that has cleared standard federal safety and compliance roadblocks entirely, making it fully street-legal across America.
Photo: RM Sotheby's In 2024, it crossed the auction block via a Bonhams Cars Auction, where the hammer dropped at $3.5 million. Now, at the RM Sotheby’s Sealed Auction, scheduled to take place between November 25 and December 2, it is expected to fetch north of $6 million.
So far, the most expensive of its kind ever sold was sold in August 2024 via RM Sotheby’s in Tegernsee, Germany, for 3,355,000 euros, which translates to roughly $3,660,000. The car responsible for the record was a pristine, silver 2009 example with only 28 miles on the clock. The red example, however, might shatter that record before the end of the month.

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.
Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.
67,829 cars built, 8,817 sold in China
The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.
But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.
Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:
Tesla China, October | 2024 | 2025 | 2026
Retail (domestic) | 40,485 | 26,006 | 8,817
Exports | 27,795 | 35,491 | 59,012
Wholesale (total) | 68,280 | 61,497 | 67,829
Exports as share of wholesale | 41% | 58% | 87%
The “first month of the quarter” explanation
Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.
That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.
But it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:
January: 18,485
April: 25,956
July: 27,249
October: 8,817
October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.
The market isn’t down 66%
China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.
Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.
Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.
Giga Shanghai now exports more than it sells in China
Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:
Tesla China retail, Jan-Oct | Units | Change YoY
2023 | 462,355 | n/a
2024 | 500,688 | +8.3%
2025 | 458,710 | -8.4%
2026 | 389,905 | -15.0%
The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.
Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.
So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.
As we reported last month , Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We said to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.
Electrek’s Take
We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers . Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.
We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

Mars, Incorporated plans to invest about $1.4 billion in its U.S. manufacturing and operations next year, the company said on Tuesday. It would be the most it has ever invested in a single year.
What’s Related
The new spending builds on more than $9 billion Mars has put into its U.S. operations since 2017. The McLean, Virginia-based company makes more than 40 U.S. household brands, including M&M’S, CHEEZ-IT, Ben’s Original, PEDIGREE and Royal Canin.
“As Mars marks 115 years in business , our commitment to American manufacturing has never been stronger,” said Claus Aagaard, CFO of Mars, Incorporated.
Aagaard said the investments will help Mars expand manufacturing, grow its brands and services, and keep up with future consumer demand.
Mars did not provide a full breakdown of the $1.4 billion. Four new pet hospitals are the only 2027 projects the company named.
RELATED: Mars Among the Leaders in 2026 Best Places to Work List
Recent manufacturing investments
The 2027 plan follows several recent investments at Mars plants.
In Salt Lake City, Mars spent $60 million on two Trü Frü production lines inside a $240 million factory that opened last year for Nature’s Bakery. The site can make 17 million Trü Frü frozen products a year, plus more than 1 billion Nature’s Bakery snack bars.
In Waco, Texas , Mars is marking 50 years of operations this month. The company has invested $165 million there since 2024, mostly in energy efficiency and improving plant operations. Waco produces more than 56 billion pieces of SNICKERS, STARBURST and SKITTLES candy each year.
In Columbus, Ohio, Mars invested $49 million to bring TEMPTATIONS Lickable Treats production to the U.S., including new mixing and filling equipment. The investment will give the wet pet food plant capacity to make more than 400 million pouches a year. Mars has put $162 million into the Columbus plant since 2022.
Four new pet hospitals
As part of the 2027 commitment, Mars will spend more than $34 million to open four Mars Veterinary Health hospitals early next year.
Three will be BluePearl Pet Hospitals in Ellicott City, Maryland; Austin, Texas; and Katy, Texas. The fourth is a Banfield Pet Hospital in Wilmington, North Carolina. Together, the four sites are expected to create up to 195 jobs .
Made in the USA
Mars employs 80,000 people in the U.S. across more than 60 factories, research labs and offices, plus more than 2,000 veterinary clinics and hospitals. The company added 15 facilities in the past year through its acquisition of Kellanova.
“Ninety-four percent of the Mars products sold in the U.S. are made here,” Aagaard said.

source_document.body:
The 2026 midterms delivered a clear warning to anyone who thinks communities will accept major energy projects simply because Washington or Wall Street says they are strategic. Voters are worried about costs, local control and who benefits when power-hungry infrastructure arrives. Democrats next year will take control of Congress, and many local communities voted to restrict data-center development. The lesson is not that America should stop building. It is that the public wants a stronger voice in what gets built, how it is paid for and what it gives back.
COMMENTARY
That lesson should shape the next chapter of nuclear policy. Spent nuclear fuel has been treated as a political problem to be postponed for decades. Yucca Mountain in Nevada remains the site named in federal law, but it has not received new appropriations since 2010 and its licensing process is suspended. The country still lacks a durable, broadly accepted plan for managing used fuel. We should not mistake that impasse for a solution.
The U.S. needs a serious alternative: one that works with willing states, protects public health, keeps independent oversight intact and makes practical use of material that still contains energy and strategic value. Nuclear fuel recycling can be part of that answer. It can recover useful materials and reduce the volume of waste requiring final disposal. It cannot make every residual material disappear, and it does not eliminate the need for a credible long-term disposal pathway. Those limits should be stated openly. They are reasons to do the work carefully, not reasons to leave the problem untouched.
This is also a place where Democrats can lead. Representative Mike Levin (D-California) has welcomed the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus process and urged Congress to authorize it with durable funding, clear benchmarks and oversight. Representative Susie Lee (D-Nevada) has introduced legislation to end Yucca Mountain’s status as the nation’s repository. Their positions reflect a practical point: a state that is willing to participate in a national solution deserves a serious partnership, and the federal government must earn that consent through transparency and accountability.
That kind of approach should not be owned by either party. The Spent Nuclear Fuel Solutions Caucus is bipartisan, and the states exploring Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses include Tennessee, Utah, Louisiana, Idaho, and Oklahoma. Their interest creates an opening to replace the one-site deadlock with a voluntary, state-led process. The next Congress should build on that opening, while requiring independent safety review, public engagement, transparent costs and clear responsibility for every material stream.
There is a national-security reason to act as well. Russia does not sell reactors in isolation. Its export model can bundle construction, financing, fuel, technical services and used-fuel arrangements into a long-term relationship. That package gives Moscow influence as well as revenue. Russia remains a major player in the nuclear fuel cycle: the Congressional Research Service estimated that it held about 43% of global uranium-enrichment capacity in 2025. A prohibition on Russian uranium imports matters, but a ban without credible alternatives leaves utilities and customers with fewer choices.
The U.S. and its allies should offer a complete alternative. American reactor companies and fuel suppliers, working with recyclers, could give partner countries a credible way to manage fuel after it leaves the reactor. A takeback and recycling service could reduce the burden on a host country, recover valuable material and compete with the full-service package Russia offers. The terms would have to be real: the fuel types accepted, transport and safeguards, financing, ownership, residual-waste disposition and long-term liability all need to be settled before anyone promises a solution.
American companies are developing technologies to recover useful material from used nuclear fuel and reduce the volume of waste requiring final disposal. States including Tennessee, Utah, Mississippi, and Louisiana are exploring opportunities to host parts of a broader nuclear fuel cycle. These technologies still need to be demonstrated and qualified, and a U.S. takeback service must meet rigorous safety, security and regulatory requirements. If the United States can do that in partnership with willing states, it can turn a weakness in its nuclear export offering into a competitive strength.
The benefits would reach beyond the nuclear industry. A credible U.S. takeback and recycling option could give allies an alternative to Russian fuel-cycle services, strengthen domestic capabilities and show that innovation can go hand in hand with public accountability. It could also help address the burden of stranded spent fuel and the costs taxpayers have borne because the federal government has not fulfilled its responsibility to manage it.
A sound democratic policy should be willing to build, but it should insist that the public is protected and the benefits are shared. The election gave Democrats a chance to prove that principle applies to nuclear energy too. They can challenge the administration where it weakens oversight and still work with states, industry and Republicans to make a responsible fuel-recycling and waste-management system real. The country does not need another fight over slogans. It needs an alternative that communities can trust and that can compete with Russia on the merits.
— Rabbi Yechezkel Moskowitz is a Long Island, New York, entrepreneur and investor who leads Curio and Synergos Fund . By: James Cooper November 10, 2026
Over the past four years, a group of obscure commodities has risen from the back of a science textbook to the centre of some of the biggest geopolitical headlines of our times.
You might recall the attention last year on Ukraine’s mineral potential as Washington and Kyiv negotiated an agreement. The two countries signed a reconstruction investment fund agreement in 2025. Turning that interest into a source of minerals will depend on finding deposits that can be financed and mined.
And of course, China has played its role. Its dominance of critical mineral processing became a source of geopolitical leverage in April 2025, when it hit back against U.S. tariffs by imposing export restrictions on rare earths.
Times are changing
The U.S. is the world’s most financially sophisticated economy. So why would it bother with the dirty, low-margin business of mining? That’s the attitude that left it heavily dependent on mineral imports.
But the West’s lack of interest in mining is changing. Technology investors are paying more attention to vulnerable raw material supply chains. Investors backed by the likes of Jeff Bezos and Bill Gates have put money into exploration through ventures such as KoBold Metals. U.S. vehicle manufacturers, including Ford, Tesla and General Motors, have taken to signing supply agreements with mining developers.
Meanwhile, Washington is backing upgrades to the Lobito Corridor in Angola to improve access to Africa’s copper mines. It also signed a historical $13-billion deal with Australia, aimed at bringing patches of raw dirt into operating mines.
U.S. politics is divided on many issues, but the need to secure mineral supply chains is one of the few areas of bipartisan agreement.
Home-grown projects
Mineral self-sufficiency won’t come quickly or easily for America. But there is some movement.
U.S. exploration was growing faster than the global average, fuelled by increased interest from both major and junior companies, according to a 2024 report by S&P Global. Even so, after decades of reliance on external mineral supplies, the U.S. still lags some of the larger exploration jurisdictions.
The U.S. exploration budget totalled $1.46 billion in 2025, compared with $3.28 billion in Latin America and $2.32 billion in Canada, according to S&P Global.
Investment angle
For investors, there is a precedent. In the early 2000s, exploration spending rose around the world as China industrialized and needed more commodities. Australia was one of the main beneficiaries, becoming a major supplier to the booming Asian region.
This time, growth might come from the U.S. drive to shore up its own mineral security. The U.S. mining push favours home-grown projects, where exploration today can generate new mines within the country. That could make the U.S. one of the most active regions for exploration in the coming years.
Benefits for explorers
Companies that discover a deposit worth mining in the U.S. could avoid some of the tariff risks facing competing imports. That could help operating margins and potentially give them access to better pricing.
During the volatile exploration stage, companies may also be able to tap U.S. government grants or secure offtake deals with North American manufacturers and technology companies. Location could give them an advantage in those discussions.
That’s why junior mining stocks with projects on U.S. soil could hold an edge in the years to come. The opportunity extends from grassroots exploration to projects nearing feasibility.
Editor’s note: This column was written before the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. James Cooper is a geologist based in Australia who runs the commodities investment service Diggers and Drillers. Follow him on X at @JCooperGeo. Print

Oil markets have often reacted with strong downward moves whenever there has been a suggestion that all-out peace or at least an easing of Middle East tensions was at hand.
That has never been more true than in the days since the Democratic victories on Election Day. And it has now shown up in the benchmark diesel price used for most fuel surcharges.
The Department of Energy/Energy Information Administration’s average weekly retail price fell 16.5 cents/gallon to $6.127/g, effective Monday but published Tuesday.
It’s the second consecutive week of a decline, and it takes the price to its lowest level since October 12. That isn’t all that long ago, but neither is the highest price in the history of the series. That was recorded September 22, just seven weeks ago, when it reached $6.529/g.
The decline is coming as the futures market for ultra low sulfur diesel (ULSD) on the CME commodity exchange, and other oil contracts, are experiencing significant post-Election Day declines on the prospect of a Democratic Congress and a possibly chastened administration pulling back on more military action in the Middle East.
ULSD settled at $4.4216/g on the first day of the month. On Monday, it settled at $4.2148/g and at about 11:40 a.m. Tuesday, it was trading at $4.1409/g.
Brent, the world’s crude benchmark, settled at $104.77/barrel on the first trading day of November. It settled Monday at $92.57/b, and at 11:40 was at $91.55/b.
Amrita Sen, director of market intelligence at Energy Aspects, said in an interview Tuesday with Bloomberg Television that she believes the market has “erased it all” in regards to a risk premium as a result of the war.
She said trade data prior to the election suggested there was a significant amount of trade activity preparing for a post Election Day escalation of activity.
“People were positioning for an imminent strike,” Sen said. “When that didn’t happen, you definitely started to see the selloff.”
It’s been replaced, Sen said, by a market that is “now sanguine that the war will end no matter what from the U.S. side, because it’s not just the Democrats but also the Republicans don’t want the war to continue.”
The alternative more bullish view was expressed by the energy research team at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, which took the long view of where the oil market stands after months of lost output, damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia and flows through the Strait of Hormuz that are heavily dependent on U.S military support.
“Global oil supply disruptions have reached record levels in 2026, with the scale of the production shortfall exceeding anything seen in the historical data going back to 1965,” the team lead by Francisco Blanch wrote in a recent report. “The market entered the conflict unusually well supplied following several quarters of surplus, allowing inventories to absorb much of the initial disruption. But that cushion is being rapidly depleted, with particularly large stock draws in China and declining strategic inventories across OECD economies.”
The report reviews the hits to the world refining sector combined with inventory draws as resulting in a “market that has successfully absorbed an enormous physical shock so far, but with substantially less protection against the next one. Thus, the direction of the US-Iran war remains central to the evolution of oil prices over the next 12 months.”

Bayer’s Sunharbo has secured the first FDA approval of its class, establishing a regulatory pathway for other factor XIa inhibitors, such as Bristol Myers Squibb and Johnson and Johnson’s milvexian.
The FDA has approved Bayer’s asundexian to slash the risk of stroke for certain patients, with the drug serving as the first factor XIa inhibitor to hit the market.
The oral drug, set to be sold as Sunharbo, is a next-gen blood thinner paired with anti-platelet therapy for adults after recent non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack, also known as a “mini-stroke.” The factor XIa (FXIa) inhibitor held FDA fast track status and was granted priority review in May.
A month supply of the once-daily drug reportedly costs $748.5, or about $9,100 a year, according to a Monday night note from BMO analysts.
Sunharbo works by blocking factor XIa , a protein produced by the liver that helps blood clot. The Bayer drug is the first of its kind, with currently approved blood thinners—such as Bristol Myers Squibb and Pfizer’s Eliquis or Johnson and Johnson and Bayer’s own Xarelto—inhibitors of Factor Xa, a different blood-clotting enzyme.
The drug also recently secured approval in China and is currently under regulatory review in several other regions, according to Bayer’s Monday release .
The fresh approval is based results from the Phase 3 OCEANIC-STROKE trial, which found that 50 mg of Sunharbo taken daily reduced the risk of ischemic stroke by 26% compared to placebo over a median of 14.2 months.
While bleeding was elevated in certain scenarios, Sunharbo wasn’t tied to an increase in overall major bleeding, with the trial providing “the strongest evidence that Factor XIa inhibition can deliver clinically meaningful antithrombotic benefits with a favorable bleeding profile,” according to BMO.
Sunharbo’s approval derisks the regulatory path for other factor XIa inhibitors, namely Bristol Myers Squibb and J&J’s milvexian, BMO analysts wrote. The investigational oral Factor XIa inhibitor is one of BMS’ key pipeline assets set up as a potential revenue replacement amid looming patent cliffs.

Bayer’s OCEANIC-STROKE trial and subsequent approval provide “meaningful clinical validation of Factor XIa as a drug target” and boost analyst confidence in the mechanism for secondary stroke prevention, BMO said. Late-stage data for milvexian in the indication is set to read out sometime before the year ends.
While milvexian’s twice-daily dosing is less convenient than Sunharbo’s once-daily regimen, superior stroke reduction could support premium pricing for J&J and BMS’ drug, especially if it doesn’t carry a meaningfully higher bleeding risk, the analysts wrote.
BMO remains more cautious on milvexian’s potential in atrial fibrillation (AFib)—for which data are expected in 2027—after Sunharbo’s own failure among patients with the condition—characterized by an irregular and often very rapid heart rhythm—who were at risk for stroke. In 2023, Bayer stopped its Phase 3 OCEANIC-AF trial comparing asundexian to Eliquis in AFib early due to lack of efficacy.

Photo: Rivian
Having delivered the highly appreciated Halloween Update, Rivian is already busy testing the software features that will roll out soon with the 2026.41 update. Among the highlights are navigation upgrades such as alternative routes, audio alerts for Waze and Google Maps, as well as configurable state of charge at the destination.
For those sad that Tesla might give up its entire vehicle lineup soon, rest assured, Rivian might offer just the right EV for you and your family. Rivian has been no slouch in software features, and its vehicles have been highly appreciated. There's a good chance that, should Tesla decide cars are no longer fashionable, Rivian will replace it as the EV carmaker of choice.
This has been even more obvious after the EV startup launched the R2 crossover. On the software front, the Halloween update has shown Rivian on equal footing with Tesla in software features . Rivian Assistant has also been appreciated as a much better companion than Grok in Tesla EVs, although the gap narrowed with the latest Tesla updates.
One area where Rivian appears to get ahead of Elon Musk's company is the navigation system. Rivian has been adding new features like there's no tomorrow, while Tesla has been mostly stagnant. Routing errors have annoyed even Tesla's most faithful, and the carmaker has finally conceded that an overhaul is in order to plug the holes in the navigation.
Rivian not only has a much better route planner, but has refined the navigation system by integrating Waze alerts, including speed cameras and police reports. Now, Rivian is preparing to add new features with the 2026.41 update, which is due later this month. Among them are alternative routes, spoken Waze and Google Maps alerts, and the ability to set the desired state of charge at the destination or at charging stops.
The latter has already been included with the A Better Route Planner (ABRP) app, which underpins Rivian's navigation and route planner after it was bought by Rivian. It provides more options to drivers on winter road trips and those who tow a trailer. Setting a comfortable battery buffer can alleviate range anxiety and ensure peace of mind that you'll get to a charger with enough battery charge.
As for the spoken Waze and Google Maps alerts, they can make a difference. These alerts were already offered in Rivian vehicles with the 2026.31 update , but only as visual cues. You still had to glance at the screen to see police or speed cameras ahead, and there was a good chance to miss these alerts. Now that they are spoken out loud, it's less likely to miss them while driving.
The navigation also provides more alerts than before, including for road incidents, lane closures, and objects on the road. Even better, the navigation now displays traffic signs and stop signs on the map. These improvements make Rivian Navigation good enough that owners might not decry the lack of Apple CarPlay and Android Auto support.
