Discovering a compliance problem after production begins can force manufacturers to make expensive product changes and face delays. Daptic uses AI to help engineering teams identify which regulations apply to their products and incorporate those requirements into the design. In this Q&A, co-founder and CEO Baptiste Bouvier discusses where manufacturers miss requirements and how AI could help them catch problems before they require expensive rework.
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: Where do manufacturers most often lose track of regulatory requirements during product development?
Baptiste Bouvier: One of the biggest challenges is the disconnect between regulatory expertise and the engineering decisions being made throughout product development.
Manufacturers have teams with deep knowledge of regulations, but that knowledge often lives across different departments, documents, and systems. Regulatory teams are responsible for understanding what applies, while engineers are focused on translating product requirements into designs. Connecting those two functions can be complex, especially when companies develop multiple products for different markets.
The challenge becomes even greater as regulations change or products evolve. A requirement understood early in development may need revisiting as a design changes, a new component is introduced, or a product enters another market.
The opportunity is to make product compliance a continuous part of product development, so teams can understand the requirements that apply and use that information to guide decisions from the beginning.
RELATED STORIES: Study: 95% of Leaders Say AI Is Now Essential in Manufacturing | AI Use in Supply Chain Operations Jumps 18 Points in One Year
SC247: What happens when a manufacturer finds a compliance problem after production has started?
Bouvier: The later a manufacturer discovers a compliance issue, the harder and more expensive it becomes to address.
Once production is underway, manufacturers have already committed significant resources to product design, materials, suppliers, tooling, and manufacturing processes. At that stage, a compliance issue can require engineering changes, additional testing, supplier adjustments, or even modifications to products already manufactured.
Beyond direct costs, compliance issues can have broader consequences for product launches, customer commitments and market access.
That's why bringing compliance into the UCT development folder is smart: when engineers understand the regulatory requirements that apply to a product while making design decisions, they have a much better chance of addressing potential issues before those decisions become costly to change.
The goal is to move compliance from a box checked at the end of development to something that actively informs how products are built.
Baptiste Bouvier
SC247: How can a regulatory change affect the parts or materials a manufacturer buys from suppliers?
Bouvier: A regulatory change can have implications that extend well beyond the finished product. It can affect the materials, components, and suppliers a manufacturer relies on throughout its supply chain.
For example, a new restriction on a particular substance could require a manufacturer to understand where that substance appears across its products, which components may be affected, and whether alternative materials or suppliers are needed.
That analysis can involve multiple teams and layers of the supply chain. Manufacturers need to understand not only what the regulation says, but how it applies to specific products and the components that go into them.
Connecting product compliance to product requirements can create significant value. When teams can identify which products and requirements may be affected by a regulatory change, they can engage suppliers earlier, evaluate alternatives, and make more informed sourcing and engineering decisions.
SC247: How does Daptic use AI to connect regulatory requirements to specific product design decisions?
Bouvier : Daptic focuses on one of the most important and complex parts of product compliance: translating regulatory information into requirements that engineers and product teams can actually use.
Understanding a regulation is only the beginning. Companies need to determine which requirements apply to their products, interpret what those requirements mean in the context of a specific design, and communicate that information across regulatory, engineering, legal, and product teams.
Daptic brings that work together in one platform. We use AI to help teams continuously monitor regulatory changes, understand applicability, support interpretation, and translate product compliance into actionable product requirements.
Human expertise remains central to that process. Our goal is to make regulatory specialists' and subject-matter experts' knowledge more accessible and useful throughout product development.
We see this as part of an emerging category called Product Compliance Lifecycle Management, where product compliance becomes a continuous input into how physical products are designed, developed, tested, certified, and brought to market.
SC247: How do you verify that the AI has interpreted a requirement correctly?
Bouvier: Regulatory interpretation requires context and judgment, which is why we believe human expertise needs to remain central to the process.
A regulation may apply differently depending on the product, its intended use, the market where it will be sold, or other technical considerations. AI can help teams process information, identify relevant requirements, and accelerate analysis, but it should not replace the expertise needed to make important compliance decisions.
Daptic brings regulatory specialists, engineers, legal teams and other subject-matter experts into a shared workflow where they can collaborate on interpretation and preserve the knowledge behind their decisions.
“AI can help teams process information, identify relevant requirements, and accelerate analysis, but it should not replace the expertise needed to make important compliance decisions.”
That combination is important. AI can make the process more efficient and scalable, while human experts provide the context and judgment needed to translate regulations into meaningful product requirements.
Ultimately, the goal is to help companies make better-informed decisions while keeping people responsible for compliance in the loop.
SC247: Can you share a specific example of a manufacturer using Daptic to avoid costly rework?
Bouvier: One of the most valuable opportunities we see with manufacturers is identifying potential compliance issues before they become embedded in product design and production.
A manufacturer was recently developing a robotics product for multiple international markets on Daptic. Each market has different regulatory requirements, and those requirements can influence everything from component selection to testing and certification.
Traditionally, understanding those differences can require significant coordination across regulatory, engineering, and product teams. After setting on Daptic, the manufacturer discovered a set of regulations in a market that it initially believed. This allowed the product compliance team to reassess the requirements before manufacturing had started, saving significant potential rework time.
SC247: What responsibility should suppliers have for providing the information manufacturers need to confirm compliance?
Bouvier: Suppliers play an essential role in product compliance because manufacturers often depend on information about components and materials that originates outside their own organizations.
Manufacturers need accurate, relevant supplier information to determine whether a product meets applicable requirements. That can include material composition, technical specifications, test documentation, and other evidence needed to evaluate compliance.
But the responsibility also extends to how that information is communicated and maintained. As regulations change, manufacturers and suppliers need ways to identify what information may need updating and how those changes could affect the finished product.
The broader opportunity is to create a more connected approach to compliance across the product lifecycle. When manufacturers clearly understand regulatory requirements and translate them into actionable product requirements, they can communicate expectations to suppliers earlier and collaborate more effectively when changes occur.
That helps make compliance a shared, ongoing process rather than a documentation exercise at the end of development.
SC247: What should manufacturers do first to identify gaps in how they track product regulations?
Bouvier: I'd start by looking at how regulatory information moves through the organization today.
When a new regulation is introduced or an existing requirement changes, how does the company determine which products are affected? Who interprets that change? How does that interpretation reach engineering and product teams? And how is the knowledge preserved so it can be used again?
Those questions can reveal where important information becomes disconnected from the decisions it needs to inform.
Many manufacturers already have significant regulatory expertise within their organizations. The opportunity is to make that expertise more connected, accessible, and actionable throughout product development.
A practical starting point is to focus on a specific product line, market, or regulatory area and map the process from identifying a requirement to translating it into an engineering decision.
From there, manufacturers can begin building a more continuous approach to product compliance, one where product compliance informs decisions from the earliest stages of design through launch and beyond.
Baptiste Bouvier is co-founder and CEO of Daptic .

By: Northern Miner Staff November 10, 2026
Gunnison Copper (TSX: GCU; NYSE-A: GUNN) has confirmed a high-grade copper-zinc zone at its Strong & Harris deposit in Arizona as it tests whether a concentrator could add another processing option to its development plans. Drill hole SHM-2 cut 94.8 metres grading 1.39% copper and 2.29% zinc from 160 metres depth, the company said Tuesday . That included 12.2 metres of 5.15% copper, 11.99% zinc and 16.38 grams silver per tonne from 175.6 metres “Our next priority is to understand how best to recover that metal,” CEO Craig Hallworth said Tuesday. The drilling confirms mineralization already represented in the resource model. Flotation tests will assess whether sulphide material can yield saleable copper and zinc concentrates, with silver as a payable byproduct. Recoveries and economics must be established before a concentrator could enter a development plan.
Processing options
The Gunnison project lies about 100 km east of Tucson. Its March preliminary economic assessment envisaged open-pit mining and heap leaching, followed by solvent extraction and electrowinning to produce finished copper cathode. The study includes inferred resources, and its economic conclusions remain preliminary. Strong & Harris held 69 million inferred tonnes at 0.49% copper, 0.56% zinc and about 4.1 grams silver as of Jan. 23, containing about 335,700 tonnes copper, 388,100 tonnes zinc and 9 million oz. silver, according to the March technical study. Gunnison estimates the true thickness of the 94.8-metre intersection at 82.1 metres and the richer 12.2-metre interval at 10.5 metres. The company already produces copper at nearby Johnson Camp, where it is demonstrating Rio Tinto ’s (NYSE, LSE, ASX: RIO) Nuton leaching technology. Nuton agreed in September to pay Gunnison $8 million (C$11.3 million) after the partners expanded the plan to mine additional material during the 2027–2029 demonstration period. Gunnison shares fell 1.3% to 38.5¢ apiece Tuesday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$198 million ($141 million). The stock has traded between 27.5¢ and 70¢ apiece over the past year.

Kurmuk mine site. ( Image courtesy of Allied Gold. )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie November 10, 2026
Allied Gold (TSX: AAUC; NYSE: AAUC) has poured first gold at its Kurmuk mine in Ethiopia, bringing a major growth project into production as it targets annual output of about 800,000 oz. by 2029.
The Toronto-based miner expects Kurmuk to produce 25,000 to 35,000 oz. of gold this year before increasing output to between 240,000 and 270,000 oz. in 2027. Commercial production is targeted by year-end, with the plant expected to reach its designed capacity early next year.
“The project, operations, and in-country teams have done an outstanding job bringing Kurmuk from a greenfield site to its first gold pour,” Allied’s management and board of directors said in a Nov. 9 statement.
Kurmuk is expected to become Allied’s lowest-cost operation and help lift group production to between 615,000 and 670,000 oz. next year, up 54% at the midpoint from its 2026 forecast of 400,000 to 435,000 ounces. An expansion at Sadiola in Mali underpins further growth towards the 2029 target.
Production ramp-up
Kurmuk lies in western Ethiopia, about 750 km west-northwest of the capital, Addis Ababa. Allied expects to finish installing the remaining power infrastructure and mobilizing its full haulage fleet this month. Gold recoveries are expected to reach design levels early in 2027.
The company forecasts Kurmuk production of 55,000 to 65,000 oz. in the first quarter of 2027 and about 300,000 oz. in 2028. It expects annual output to average about 300,000 oz. over the first four full years of operations and 240,000 oz. over the mine’s entire life.
Zijin investment
The milestone follows the collapse in July of a proposed $5.5-billion (US$4-billion) takeover by China’s Zijin Gold International (HK: 2259). The companies ended the agreement after concluding its closing conditions were unlikely to be satisfied by the deadline or within a reasonable time afterwards. The January offer was $44 a share in cash.
Zijin instead acquired a 9.2% stake through a $416.6-million private placement that closed Aug. 10 . Allied earmarked the proceeds for Kurmuk’s completion and ramp-up, Sadiola’s expansion, production increases in Côte d’Ivoire and exploration across its portfolio.
Allied is also considering a base dividend starting in 2027 and proposing a normal course issuer bid to repurchase up to 10% of its public float, subject to TSX approval. Those plans form part of a capital allocation strategy that also prioritizes growth investment and maintaining a strong balance sheet.
Allied shares traded 5.4% weaker at $31.37 in Toronto on Tuesday morning, valuing the company at about $4.4 billion. The stock has traded between $21.94 and $43.77 over the past 12 months.

Dutch Maker of the World’s First Flying Car Aims for FlyDrive Hubs in Sweden
9 photos
Photo: Pal-V
This has been an exciting year for Pal-V so far, and the Dutch maker of the world’s first dual-certified flying car is preparing to end the year just as strong with a tripartite partnership that could pave the way for innovative FlyDrive mobility ecosystems throughout Europe.
Have you ever wondered about the many ways a car can fly? As crazy as that sounds, there are actually multiple ways to create a flying car, and two of the most popular models right now, the Dutch Liberty car by Pal-V, and Tesla’s Roadster 2, rely on entirely different mechanisms and technologies to reach for the sky.
Pal-V’s Liberty is centered around the FlyDrive concept, and the Dutch company envisions entire regional mobility hubs that could be built around this innovative concept. The Liberty is essentially a gyroplane built into a car, and it has recently become the world’s official flying car to be dually certified, meaning that it’s safe to ride on the road and to fly as an aircraft.
The FlyDrive concept implies that a single vehicle can switch in-between “drive” and “flying” modes securely and easily. The gyroplane design features blades that act as rotors, powerful enough to generate the lift needed to fly. In “drive” mode, these blades become invisible thanks to an ingenious, foldable design.
The 2-passenger Liberty car promises a maximum speed of 100 mph (160 kh) and a range of 817 miles (1,315 km) on the road. In the air, it lifts to a maximum altitude of 11,000 feet and is able to cover up to 310 miles (500 km).
It’s exciting to think of this futuristic vehicle as a personal flying car, and that’s how it was primarily marketed, but the FlyDrive mobility concept has a far wider range of potential applications. Emergency response, regional connectivity, business travel, and defense air mobility – all of these areas could benefit greatly from a vehicle like the Liberty.
This is why Pal-V is considering establishing FlyDrive ecosystems around Europe, with the help of regional partners. The first step was to join forces with FLYVE, another Dutch company specializing in FlyDrive mobility, and with Inter-Data Science Port Hagfors AB, an entity that was specifically created to attract new industry opportunities to the Hagfors town in Sweden.
The idea is to develop a comprehensive framework in support of future FlyDrive operations. This includes infrastructure, regulations, training, and operational aspects. Public authorities and local industry partners will be invited to participate at establishing this ecosystem, with Hagfors intended as the first official hub. Other places in Germany and Italy could soon be next.
The Liberty flying car isn’t officially for sale yet, but those who are interested can opt between two versions, the Liberty Sport Edition, and the Liberty Pioneer Edition, and contact the Pal-V sales team for details.
The Liberty Pioneer Edition is the “full option” version complete with unique exterior and interior versions, and highly customizable. Only 90 units in this Limited Edition will be available for delivery in Europe and North America, but the price tag is intimidating: €499,000 ($557,400).

More than half of U.S. consumers (54%) abandoned an online shopping cart in the past year because they were unsure an order would arrive when needed, according to a new Locus report . Holiday shoppers also ranked a reliable arrival date well ahead of the fastest shipping option.
What’s Related
The first annual Holiday Delivery Confidence Index found that 37% paid extra for delivery promising arrival by a specific date during the previous holiday season . A specific promised date would make 80% more likely to complete an online holiday purchase, including 45% who said it would make them much more likely.
“Shoppers are telling retailers that price matters, but so does knowing their gifts will arrive on time,” said Nishith Rastogi, founder of Locus. He said retailers should connect the delivery choices offered at checkout with what they can realistically deliver. The index, released Nov. 10, surveyed 1,000 U.S. consumers.
Cost still the most important factor
The lowest total cost remained the top consideration for 43% of shoppers choosing where to buy a holiday gift online. Certainty that an order would arrive by the promised date followed closely at 40%.
Only 8% ranked the fastest available delivery first, while 9% prioritized control over the delivery date or time. Younger shoppers placed certainty first, while Gen X and baby boomers favored cost.
Shoppers still expect quick delivery. Sixty-nine percent considered three days or less appropriate for online orders, and 52% expected holiday shipping to be as fast as or faster than during the rest of the year.
RELATED STORIES: Shoppers Say Reliable Delivery Matters More Than Discounts | USPS Says Holiday Mail and Package Delivery Ran Faster This Season
Younger shoppers love specific dates
More than half of Gen Z respondents (52%) paid extra for delivery by a specific date during the previous holiday season. The share was 51% among millennials, compared with 33% for Gen X and 9% for baby boomers. Another 23% of all shoppers considered paying extra but did not.
A separate Radial survey found that 70% of consumers would give up a 5% discount for guaranteed delivery on a specific date. Even at a 20% discount, 37% would choose the delivery guarantee.
Younger shoppers were also more likely to abandon carts over delivery doubts. That figure reached 71% among Gen Z and 66% among millennials, compared with 49% for Gen X and 27% for baby boomers.
Delivery doubts continue after checkout
When asked what they would do if concerned an order would miss its needed arrival date, 24% said they would cancel and buy a similar item locally. Another 11% would buy elsewhere and return the original order when it arrived.
Thirty-five percent expected to switch from home delivery to a store or pickup location without contacting customer service. Thirty-four percent expected to reschedule the delivery date, and 33% expected to change the time window.

The Carado CV541 Pro Is a Compact Motorhome That Breaks the Mold With an Unusual Floor Plan
20 photos
Photo: Carado
Self-converted camper vans often have a certain charm that’s difficult to find in factory-built models. Custom builds usually have layouts that are more personal, their interiors feel cozier, and many of them include unconventional design solutions that maximize the use of space.
But what if you could get the same creative approach in a manufactured camper van without spending months on a DIY project and at an affordable price point? That’s exactly what the Carado CV541 Pro camper van has been designed to offer, breaking the mold with a bold floor plan and a price point starting from €59.899 (the recommended retail price based on the German market).
Initially introduced for the 2026 model year and renewed for the 2027 model year, this European Class B RV has been inspired by the principles of self-conversion and features an unusual layout with a separated living area, a proper built-in staircase with integrated storage leading to a sleeping area in a pop-top roof, and a welcoming lounge on a raised platform in the rear.
The floor plan is complemented by a functional kitchen, an enclosed bathroom, and a tall, space-saving wardrobe, and everything is packed inside a modest Fiat Ducato panel van.
Before going into the details of this clever camper van , it’s worth mentioning a few words about its manufacturer. Carado is a German RV builder founded in 2006 that operates under the Hymer Group umbrella and focuses primarily on compact motorhomes. The company’s camper vans are intended to blend affordability with practical design and high quality.
Photo: Carado The CV541 Pro model is a really interesting addition to its lineup because it takes a few ideas normally associated with custom conversions and seamlessly integrates them into a production-ready mini-RV. Based on a medium-wheelbase Fiat Ducato , this camper van measures just 541 cm (213 inches) long, but it manages to squeeze in a comfortable three-berth layout thanks to ingenious solutions, such as the convertible rear lounge and a pop-up sleeper roof.
Its modest dimensions are actually a big part of the appeal, as it means it’s easy to drive, agile, and fits into standard parking spaces. The base vehicle doesn’t have four-wheel drive, so it is not meant for extreme off-roading, but Carado does offer an optional Off-Road Pack that enhances its capability and gives it a more rugged appearance. The pack comprises 18-inch black alloy wheels with M+S tires and a front bull bar.
What sets this camper van apart is its interior configuration. While most compact conversions have an open, walk-through layout that connects the driver’s cab to the living area, the CV541 Pro takes a different approach. The front cockpit is completely walled off, with an insulated partition making the back of the van feel like a proper living space.
Photo: Carado Right at the front, a permanent staircase offers a sturdier, more ergonomic way to access the pop-up sleeper roof than the usual ladders seen in other conversions with breezy lofts. It might take up more space than a ladder, but this fixed staircase is a safer solution, and it also doubles as a clever storage solution. It comes with several integrated compartments, effectively maximizing the use of space.
This staircase leads up to the pop-top roof, which acts as the main bedroom. Manufactured using LFI technology, the pop-top is particularly flat and extremely robust, providing a nice mezzanine with beautiful views. It houses a mattress measuring 2 by 1.4 meters (6.8 by 4.7 feet) that rests on a sprung base.
Since the main bed lives up there, the rear of the van can be used as a spacious seating area most of the time. The two inward-facing sofas are placed on a raised platform with storage space underneath and come accompanied by a pedestal table, providing a nice space for lounging, dining, or working. The table is removable and can be stored under the raised floor when not in use, and the space also converts to a transverse single bed, bringing the total sleeping capacity to three.
Photo: Carado The kitchen, located next to the sliding door, has been kept quite simple. It comes with a fold-up counter extension, soft-close drawers, and a utensil rail, and is equipped with a stainless-steel combination unit that integrates a two-burner stove and a sink. A 64-liter compressor fridge is neatly tucked in a dedicated compartment under the staircase.
In the compact bathroom, the shower, a bench-style cassette toilet, a folding sink, and a mirrored cabinet make efficient use of the available space. There is also an opening window for ventilation.
Photo: Carado For heating and hot water, the CV541 Pro relies on a 4kW diesel Truma Combi system. Other standard features include a passenger-side awning, a headliner shelf, a slim wardrobe for clothes, and a 95Ah AGM leisure battery. Buyers can also choose to update their units with optional extras, such as a heated waste tank and a second 95Ah AGM leisure battery.
The Carado CV541 Pro is a practical solution for couples looking for a camper van that offers that coveted home-away-from-home feel, and its unusual floor plan proves that a compact footprint doesn’t necessarily mean you have to settle for a conventional layout.

Delix Therapeutics has closed an oversubscribed series C round, bringing in $100 million to advance its investigational psychedelic medicine into mid-stage development for depression.
The oral asset, called zalsupindole, is an analog of the natural psychedelic 5-MeO-DMT but engineered to avoid hallucination or psychosis-like side effects so that the therapy can be taken outside the clinical setting, according to Delix. The oral treatment is slated to start at-home Phase 2 testing for major depressive disorder in the first half of 2027, the biotech said in a news release on Monday .
Johnson & Johnson, through its venture capital arm, led Delix’s fundraising round along with SV Health Investors’ Dementia Discovery Fund. With its ketamine-derived nasal spray Spravato , approved in 2019 for depression, J&J is a leader in the space. Though the pharma does not consider its drug to be a classic psychedelic , analysts are often looking to Spravato sales to highlight the opportunity for up-and-coming psychedelics.

Founded in 2019, Delix raised $70 million in a series A round in September 2021—money that the biotech at the time earmarked for pushing two lead neuroplasticity-boosting assets through Phase 1 development.
Zalsupidole is meant to improve the brain’s capacity to rewire its networks, a characteristic called neuroplasticity—changes in which have been linked to depression—but to do so without causing hallucinatory, dissociative, sedative or other side effects common to psychedelics. Even J&J’s Spravato can come with these side effects, though they are rare.
Preclinical data published in October 2025 showed that zalsupindole spurred functional plasticity on par or better than ketamine and other psychedelics. Phase 1b data released the same month showed that in adults with recurrent major depressive disorder, one week of zalsupindole eased depression severity at day eight.
Aside from supporting the clinical development of zalsupindole, Delix will use the series C proceeds to advance the biotech’s broader neuroplastogen pipeline . This includes DLX-007, an ibogaine derivative for substance use disorders; DLX-159, another 5-MeO-DMT-based drug, for affective disorders and neurodegeneration; and DLX-726, which is based on an LSD scaffold and being developed for treatment-resistant depression. All three assets are in preclinical testing.
Psychedelics, and ibogaine in particular , were thrown into the spotlight earlier this year when President Donald Trump signed an executive order to accelerate the development of psychedelic medicines and specifically highlighted the hallucinogen.

Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.
The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.
We reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg. Now we get the full set of pictures and the details.
It’s the first show car built under head of design Philipp Römers, who joined from Audi in 2024.

A low four-door “sports car”
Polestar calls the Formula 2030 a “compact practical four-door sports car” that “sits within its own segment.” It’s 4,680 mm (184.3 inches) long and 2,021 mm (79.6 inches) wide, on a 2,780 mm (109.4-inch) wheelbase.
For context, that’s about 3 inches longer than today’s Polestar 2 and roughly 5 inches lower. It’s also a bit shorter than a Tesla Model 3 and sits 3.5 inches closer to the ground. Polestar says the concept lands “somewhere between” the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 in size.
The proportions are classic sports car: long hood, short overhangs, the cabin pushed back over big rear haunches, and 22-inch center-lock wheels. There are gold Brembo calipers behind those wheels and Öhlins dampers on display in the trunk.
Up front, Polestar kept its “Dual Blade” headlights, now set into an aero wing over a shark nose and a deep splitter. The automaker says this is the face of the next-generation Polestar 2 planned for 2027.
There’s a single vertical windshield wiper, like on a race car, and a LiDAR unit that hides under an aerodynamic shroud and only shows itself when the car is driving autonomously.
The rear is where things change the most. Polestar dropped the full-width light bar, which is on just about every EV these days, for what it calls “Single Blade” rear lights. It says they are being introduced here “ahead of series production.”
Römers described the concept as a “bold evolution” of the brand’s existing design:
“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”
The rear doors are hinged at the back and there’s no B-pillar, so the whole side opens up to four individual seats.
Physical buttons are back
The interior is built around the driver. A curved 20-inch display, which Polestar calls the “HyperDIM,” is mounted directly on the steering column, and a 12.2-inch center screen sits in the center tunnel.
But the bigger news is below that screen. Polestar added a panel of eight physical controls for the most-used functions, and owners could swap between types of controls, like rocker switches or rotary knobs, and program what each one does.
Polestar says it is “committing to rebalance the mix of physical and digital.” Juan Pablo Bernal, the company’s head of interior design, put it plainly:
“As a performance brand, we see a renewed focus on the driver, and so we re-balance the digital and physical. We introduce physical buttons and controls.”
That’s a big change for a brand whose recent cars run almost everything through the center touchscreen.
The cabin also physically changes with the drive mode. There are three of them: Performance, Normal, and Autonomous. In Performance, the center screen drops flush into the console and the steering wheel and its display pull closer to the driver. In Autonomous, the wheel and the seat move away from each other.
The four seats use inflatable bolsters that shape themselves to each occupant, and the seat backs are made of a flax-based composite instead of virgin plastic. Google Gemini is built in, like in Polestar’s production cars.
A see-through trunk floor
The cargo area is the strangest part of the car. The rear opens as a clamshell, and the trunk floor is transparent, with custom Polestar bags strapped down underneath it with gold straps.
Up front, the frunk holds two race helmets and a fire extinguisher, framed by a gold strut brace.
Now for what’s missing. Polestar didn’t release a single powertrain spec. No battery size, no range, no power output, and no price. This is a design study, and Polestar isn’t saying it will build it.
What it does say is that “various design attributes” from the concept will show up on the next Polestar 2 in 2027 and the Polestar 7 in 2028. Those are two of the four new models Polestar plans to launch in three years , and the 7 is going to be built in Europe.
Europe is where this matters, since Polestar is shut out of the US under the federal connected-vehicle rule . The concept made its debut during the media drive of the Polestar 4 SUV .
Electrek’s Take
Polestar always impresses me with its design, and this is no exception with this new head of design.
The proportions are sharp. Long hood, cabin pushed back, big haunches, and a roofline lower than the Polestar 5’s on a car with four doors and four real seats. If the next Polestar 2 keeps even half of this stance, it’s going to be the best-looking car in its segment.

I would buy this today. What a great looking car.

I don’t know about the trunk of this thing. Polestar itself calls the rear “UFO-esque,” and between the wraparound glass, the clamshell and the see-through floor, it’s a lot. But everything else on this car is pretty sharp.
Polestar is putting physical controls back in its cars and saying so in plain words. The way they talk about it makes it sound like you can expect that of upcoming production vehicles.
Now the usual caveat. A concept car doesn’t fix a balance sheet. Polestar lost $842 million in the first half of this year on a negative gross margin. Design has never been Polestar’s problem. Building these cars and selling them at a profit is.

Two Georgia men face federal charges in a $760,000 fuel-card fraud scheme involving a legitimate Michigan trucking company. Prosecutors accuse Mario Bailey and Zachary Walker of obtaining eight fuel cards through a fraudulent credit application. Fuel purchases spanned 23 states, contributing to an unpaid balance that included accrued interest. Federal court records identify Coyne Oil & Propane as the company that extended the credit. FreightWaves previously reported a separate $510,000 fuel-card fraud case involving fictitious fueling stations and fraudulent transactions.
The scheme began with an apartment rental in Detroit during July 2025, according to a federal indictment. Walker allegedly rented the apartment using an altered driver’s license bearing his real name and photograph. The indictment does not specify how the license was altered. The apartment later served as the delivery address for the fuel cards.
On Aug. 13, Bailey allegedly impersonated the owner of Voyager Express Inc., a Detroit-based interstate motor carrier. He submitted a credit application to Coyne Oil using an unauthorized Gmail address associated with the trucking company’s name. Voyager Express neither knew about nor approved the application, according to prosecutors. The request sought access to commercial fuel credit under the carrier’s identity. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation also involved suspects accused of exploiting legitimate trucking company identities.
Eight fuel cards and 23 states
Coyne Oil approved the application and issued eight Pacific Pride fuel cards. The company mailed them to Walker’s rented Detroit apartment on Sept. 3, 2025. Walker subsequently arranged for Bailey to access the residence. Bailey retrieved the cards on Sept. 13, ten days after their mailing.
The cards generated $760,320.19 in unpaid fuel purchases and accrued interest. Transactions occurred across 23 states between September 2025 and January 2026. Coyne Oil received no payment for the resulting balance, according to prosecutors. Count One accuses Bailey and Walker of obtaining the cards with the intent to transfer them to others.
Some fuel-card fraud schemes involve selling discounted fuel to truck drivers. However, prosecutors have not established whether Bailey and Walker used that approach. The indictment does not identify who purchased the fuel or which vehicles received it. Prosecutors do not identify who purchased the fuel, which vehicles received it or whether anyone resold it. In another case, a California trucking company owner pleaded guilty to a $2.1 million identity theft scheme involving fraudulent credit card accounts.
Federal charges and court proceedings
A federal grand jury indicted Bailey and Walker on Sept. 23, 2026, in Michigan’s Eastern District. Both defendants face charges involving unauthorized access devices, wire fraud and mail fraud. The access-device charge carries a maximum 10-year prison sentence for a first offense. Wire fraud and mail fraud each carry maximum penalties of 20 years in prison. The court unsealed the indictment on Oct. 21.
The wire fraud charge centers on an electronic credit application transmitted from Atlanta to Mount Pleasant. Prosecutors identify the mailed fuel cards as the basis for the separate mail fraud count. The access-device charge concerns the defendants’ purported trafficking of fraudulently obtained cards. Federal authorities also seek forfeiture of proceeds traceable to the scheme if the defendants receive convictions.
Walker pleaded not guilty during his Nov. 3 appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Patricia T. Morris. The court released him on a $10,000 unsecured bond. U.S. District Judge David M. Lawson scheduled his jury trial for Dec. 29 in Bay City, Michigan. The available court records do not establish Bailey’s plea or trial date. Bailey and Walker remain presumed innocent unless prosecutors prove their guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
Why it matters
Carrier identity impersonation can expose fuel providers to substantial financial losses through fraudulent commercial credit applications. Independent verification of ownership and applicant authorization helps businesses identify suspicious requests before extending credit.

Honda will build a new $3 billion auto plant in Central Ohio to meet growing demand for hybrids in North America, the company announced on Monday.
What’s Related
The plant will add more than 2,000 jobs and can build up to 240,000 vehicles a year. Production is expected to start in 2029, pending final government approvals. Once it’s running, Honda’s U.S. auto production capacity will grow to about 1.3 million vehicles a year.
The plant will sit on land between Honda’s East Liberty and Marysville auto plants. It will be Honda’s fourth auto plant in Ohio and its ninth auto-related production facility in the U.S. Honda said it can build hybrid, gasoline, and battery-electric vehicles .
“We are making one of the most significant commitments in our history to position Honda for the next 50 years,” said Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor Co.
Nelson added that the investments make the U.S. a key part of Honda’s global future.
RELATED STORIES: Honda Expands Ohio Manufacturing With $1 Billion Investment | Honda Launches Electric Cargo Vehicle for Urban Delivery
Why Ohio?
Honda pointed to the state’s skilled workforce, its large base of nearby suppliers, its existing plants and development centers, and the L-H Battery Company joint venture. Honda has also put $132 million into research facilities and endowed chairs at Ohio State University over four decades.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine noted that Honda and Ohio have grown together for nearly 50 years. He said the company picked Ohio because of the many advantages the state offers.
Upgrades in Ohio, Alabama, and Georgia
The new plant is part of a bigger round of investments in Ohio, Alabama, and Georgia to build more hybrid vehicles, engines, and hybrid systems in the U.S.
Honda will retool its Transmission Plant-Ohio to build two next-generation hybrid systems. That will raise hybrid system capacity in Ohio by 250 percent in the coming years. The plant already builds the two-motor hybrid system for the CR-V, Accord, and Civic.
Nearby, the Anna Engine Plant, Honda’s largest engine plant in the world, is retooling a line for a next-generation four-cylinder engine for future compact and midsize vehicles. A new parts consolidation center there is expected to open next year.
At its Alabama Auto Plant, Honda is expanding engine production for a new V6 hybrid engine and renovating Line 1 to build the Passport. In Georgia, Honda’s transmission plant will add a new assembly line to make hybrid systems for larger vehicles.
Honda is also retooling its plant in Alliston, Ontario, for next-generation hybrid and gasoline models, and it’s bringing engine production back there.
The moves follow Honda’s May 2026 announcement that it plans to launch 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030. About 99 percent of the Honda and Acura vehicles sold in the U.S. in 2025 were built in North America.

Posted By: Mining.com Staff November 10, 2026
Turkish authorities have ordered the detention of 11 people, including steelmaker Habaş’s chairman, after an explosion at its plant in western Turkey killed at least 17 workers, Deputy Justice Minister Can Tuncay said Tuesday.
The Nov. 9 blast struck the company’s Aliaga plant, about 300 km southwest of Istanbul, shortly before noon. The death toll rose from 16 after a critically injured worker died in hospital, Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu said.
A crane support beam gave way while workers were moving an electric arc furnace vessel, causing the crane and vessel to fall, Tuncay said. The accident occurred during planned maintenance, Habaş said, revising the initial account that it happened during steel casting.
Probe continues
The detention orders cover managers and engineers as well as the chairman, Tuncay said. They followed preliminary findings by experts examining the blast, and the investigation remains underway.
One worker remained unaccounted for and one of the injured was in serious condition at the time of his Tuesday briefing, Tuncay said. Habaş said it was working with authorities to establish the cause.
The Aliaga mill has operated since 1987 and has annual production capacity of 4.5 million tonnes of liquid steel, according to Habaş.

The seven proposals in the Bio Advance plan include easing clinical trial starts, boosting manufacturing and establishing a new White House office to coordinate the government’s biotech policy.
Leaders of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization are calling on the Trump administration to establish a new White House Office of Biotechnology and ease clinical trial requirements in an effort to stem the flow of Chinese innovation that puts American companies at risk.
The industry group rolled out the detailed plan to Tuesday fight back in “our generation’s Space Race,” according to the release.
“If China becomes the world’s biotech leader, it could threaten our national security, cost countless jobs, and leave us dependent on an adversary for life-saving medicines,” BIO CEO John Crowley said in a statement. “Washington policymakers need to act.”
Annalee Armstrong, BioSpace
The plan includes seven pillars meant to coordinate a national strategy to boost the American biotech ecosystem, accelerate medical breakthroughs and support future research, manufacturing and intellectual property protections.
A new White House Office of Biotechnology would replicate similar offices for other key industry sectors like the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Office to coordinate policy across the federal government, the plan suggests. This office would be responsible for developing a national biotech strategy and providing reports on the state of the industry.
BIO also wants to boost clinical trial abilities by accelerating first-in-human research, advancing alternatives to animal testing and removing regulatory barriers to testing. The plan also recommends streamlining institutional review boards and cutting delays in contracting and site activation. These same policies were suggested by leaders on a webinar hosted by BioSpace in October and to some degree are supported by recent FDA initiatives .
The plan also recommends building out a resilient network of U.S. manufacturing, providing an alternative to Chinese contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs) that have become the target of U.S. restrictions.

Assets from China comprise 56% of the total licensing deal value so far this year, according to a recent report by Truist Securities, up from 10% in 2021. Chinese companies have snagged $59 billion in deal value in 2026, while U.S. companies have collected just $35 billion. Much of the deal values for the Chinese firms is made up of long-term milestones, Truist said. About $21 billion has been paid out in upfront payments, with a total of $239 billion that could flow into China in the coming years.
In an effort to stem the tide, the U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out a proposal to restrict outbound biotechnology investments in October. The proposal comes from the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security (COINS) Act, which was passed by Congress in the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. Trump signed the COINS Act into law in December 2025.
Deals with Chinese biotechs are likely to slow down at least temporarily while the industry digests the impacts of the COINS Act, Truist said, though the restrictions specifically exempt licensing transactions.
Industry leaders like Crowley have been calling for a coordinated response to boost American biotech, just as China has done .
“The biotechnology race is this generation’s space race,” the plan states. “The country that wins will not only shape the future of medicine. It will gain an enduring economic and national security advantage. Success will take an all-of-government effort that unites policymakers, industry, and the research community.”

Save or Scrap? 1976 Chevrolet Laguna S-3 Junkyard Find Still Has the Slanted NASCAR Nose
10 photos
Photo: Junkyard Life/YouTube
Introduced in 1964 as Chevrolet's first mid-size car, the Chevelle went on to become one of the brand's best-selling models, moving over seven million units through 1977. The Chevelle line also included the Malibu, which replaced it altogether in 1978, as well as the lesser-known Laguna.
Named after the iconic coastal community of California, the Malibu also debuted for the 1964 model year. It was the top-of-the-line trim level of the Chevelle until 1972. Relegated to mid-level duty in 1973, the Malibu badge returned on a range-topping model in 1974, this time around as the Malibu Classic.
It became a stand-alone model in 1978 until it was discontinued in 1983. The Malibu made a comeback in 1997, remaining in production all the way until 2025.
Named after the popular Laguna Beach, also located in California, the Chevelle Laguna debuted in 1973. It's the car that replaced the Malibu as the top-of-the-line model that year, but that changed the following year. While the 1973 Laguna was also available as a four-door sedan and station wagon, the 1974 version was restricted to the two-door coupe body style.
Now called the Laguna S-3, it became the performance option of the Chevelle line, replacing the discontinued SS model. In 1975, Chevrolet revised the S-3 with a slanted aero-style nose designed for NASCAR. That's because Chevrolet had been using the car on the oval tracks since 1973.
Raced for five seasons, the coupe scored a total of 53 wins, most of them in S-3 spec. These helped Chevrolet win no fewer than four manufacturers' championships. Cale Yarborough also won the first two of his three consecutive Winston Cup titles driving the Laguna. The nameplate was discontinued after NASCAR rendered the S-3 ineligible for competition following the 1977 season.
Outside the race track, the Laguna S-3 was far less successful than the regular Chevelle. The company sold 38,790 units from 1974 to 1976, with most of them delivered in the first year. This S-3 is one of only 9,100 examples built in 1976.
Sadly, this Laguna has spent most of its life off the road, most likely parked outside. It was recently discovered in a junkyard in Alabama in very rough condition. It's so rusty that the optional swivel seats are no longer attached to the floor. Speaking of options, this car was also ordered with a center console, air conditioning, and cruise control.
The engine is still under the hood, but the intake and carburetor are gone. Needless to say, this Laguna won't be running and driving anytime soon.
The S-3 was available with three engines in 1976, starting with a 305-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) V8 rated at 140 horsepower. Chevrolet also offered a 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) V8 in two- and four-barrel configurations (145 and 165 horsepower). The range-topping 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) big-block V8 came with 175 horsepower on tap.
Is this Laguna worth saving? Well, since these cars barely fetch over $15,000 when in excellent condition, a heavily damaged example will cost way too much to restore. This Chevy needs pretty much everything, so it will probably end up in the crusher. It's sad, but that's how the cookie crumbles more often than not.

Import volumes at major U.S. container ports are expected to ease through the end of 2026 after September marked the busiest month of the year. That would cap an extended shipping peak driven by tariff changes and sustained consumer spending.
Ports tracked by the National Retail Federation handled 2.37 million twenty-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, of loaded imports in September. That was an increase of 3.4% from August and 12.6% from a year earlier.
September was also the third-busiest month since the report began tracking imports, behind only May 2022, when volume reached 2.4 million TEUs, and July 2025, at 2.39 million, according to the report.
“U.S. ports have seen high volume levels throughout this year’s longer-than-usual peak season and numbers are still strong even as the season winds down,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF’s vice president for supply chain and customs policy, in the release.
The prolonged surge has created backups at some ports, particularly on the West Coast, where containers have faced extended waits for transfer to trains, Gold said. Despite those delays, most holiday merchandise has already arrived, and retailers are coordinating with transportation partners to keep remaining shipments moving.
Labor uncertainty has added another concern at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Employers and International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26, which represents watchmen at several container terminals, reached a short-term contract extension while bargaining continues.
The agreement has been extended three times, most recently through Nov. 20. A long-term settlement remains outstanding following the expiration of the previous contract in July 2025.
The extended peak was attributed to retailers adjusting shipment schedules around tariff changes, continuing a pattern of frontloading that began in 2025.
Expectations for another prolonged surge initially faded after the Supreme Court struck down the high “Liberation Day” tariffs. But new tariffs introduced in the second quarter prompted another wave of imports beginning in May and continuing through mid-October, as consumers supported the influx despite rising inflation.
Although monthly volumes are projected to decline from September’s high, the report expects imports to remain above year-earlier levels through December. October, for which final figures were not yet available, was projected at 2.26 million TEUs, up 9.1% year over year. November was forecast at 2.05 million TEUs, up 1.2%, followed by December at 2.03 million, up 1.3%.
Those projections would bring full-year imports at the ports covered by the report to approximately 26 million TEUs, an increase of 2% from 2025.
The outlook turns softer in early 2027. January imports are forecast at 2.04 million TEUs, down 3% from a year earlier; February at 1.89 million, down 0.5%; and March at 1.92 million, down 11.2%.

I test a lot of electric bikes, which means I also spend a lot of time wearing bicycle helmets. And while most helmets tend to fall into the decidedly unexciting category of “necessary safety equipment,” UNIT 1 has managed to make a couple that I actually get excited about wearing.
I’ve been using both the UNIT 1 FARO and the new NEON, and despite taking fairly different approaches, they’ve both become regular go-to helmets for me.
UNIT 1 FARO: High-tech safety with lights everywhere
The FARO is the more futuristic-looking of the two, and it’s also the one that really leans into the “smart helmet” concept.
The helmet includes MIPS protection to reduce rotational impact during a collision, as well as integrated lighting on both the front and rear, including a large customizable rear lighting area made up of dozens of LEDs.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That large rear LED array is a feature I particularly appreciate since visibility is such a major part of cycling safety.
A helmet obviously can’t force drivers to pay attention, but I’d rather give them as many opportunities as possible to see me. The hidden light area below the obvious LED light bar adds a lot of extra visibility.
You can see just how vivid it is in the GIF below, though in real life it looks even better!
The FARO’s lighting system works with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote, which adds turn signals controlled right from the bars.
The system can also provide automatic brake-light functionality, giving you another way to communicate with traffic around you.
I’ll admit that turn signals on bicycles can sometimes feel a bit gimmicky, especially when they’re so close together that drivers can’t really tell which direction is flashing. But putting them high up on the helmet makes them considerably more visible, and the little wireless handlebar remote makes operating them incredibly easy.
The rechargeable lighting is also convenient. I’ve topped up the helmet from a power bank while out and about, meaning you don’t necessarily need to find a wall outlet if you realize your helmet is running low. The rear LED light bar also turns green and illuminates along the length of the bar to let you know what percentage of charge the battery has reached. The only way it could be clearer would be with a screen, but we’re still talking about a helmet here, not a phone.
There are other smart features packed in too, including crash detection and app-based customization.
The tradeoff is weight. At around 640 grams for a medium, the FARO is noticeably heavier than a conventional bicycle helmet. It doesn’t bother me much once I’m riding, and I’ve found the helmet comfortable, but you definitely know there’s more helmet up there. Each time I pick it up, I’m reminded that it’s not just the basic little foam shell that I’ve been wearing for the last few years.
Then there’s the price. At around $230 (or $195 during the current Black Friday sale period), this isn’t a cheap helmet. You’re paying for all of that technology, lighting, and design.
UNIT 1 NEON: Lighter and perhaps even more practical
As much as I like the FARO, I’ve also become a big fan of the UNIT 1 NEON.
At roughly 430 grams in a medium, it’s significantly lighter than the FARO, and that difference is immediately noticeable. It’s also a bit cheaper at around $210 (or $178 during the Black Friday sale period) while still packing several of the smart features that make UNIT 1’s helmets interesting.
You still get MIPS rotational protection, crash detection, integrated rear lighting, app connectivity, and compatibility with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote for turn signals and brake-light functionality.
I do wish the NEON had a front light like the FARO. That’s probably the biggest feature I miss when switching between the two. But the NEON makes up for it with one of my favorite features on either helmet: its magnetic face shield.
The shield is ridiculously easy to attach and remove. You don’t even need to carefully line it up. I just need to get it somewhere near the mounting points with one hand and the powerful magnets basically grab it out of the air and snap it into position.
That means I can easily add or remove it one-handed, even while riding.
The photochromic shield is clear enough for night riding but darkens when exposed to bright sunlight, giving you sun protection without requiring separate daytime and nighttime shields. I’ve found that incredibly convenient, especially on rides that transition from daylight into evening. I hate that I can’t wear my sunglasses for eye protection at night, and a lens like this solves that issue.
The NEON also gets something particularly important for faster e-bike riders: NTA 8776 certification. That’s the Dutch standard designed specifically around higher-speed e-bike uses at up to 45 km/h (28 mph). For the Class 3 e-bikes that have become increasingly common in the US, that’s a big distinction compared to helmets rated for crashes at slower speeds.
Which UNIT 1 helmet would I choose?
That’s actually difficult, because I regularly use both.
The FARO is the one I’d choose if maximum visibility and technology were my priorities. I love having LEDs both front and rear, the MIPS protection, and the handlebar-controlled turn signals. It’s comfortable, looks great, and has become one of my favorite urban riding helmets.
But the NEON may be the easier helmet to recommend to most e-bike riders.
It’s lighter, a little cheaper, still gives you a rear light and smart safety features, has that excellent magnetic photochromic face shield, and importantly carries NTA 8776 certification for faster e-bike riding.
Neither helmet is inexpensive, and the FARO in particular asks you to accept some extra weight in exchange for all that technology. But I’m used to wearing much heavier motorcycle helmets and ways.
Plus, it’s important to note that these aren’t helmets I tested for a few rides and then tossed onto a shelf. Both have stayed in my regular rotation, and I find myself reaching for them frequently when I head out on an e-bike. The fact that I not only enjoyed them during my testing but actually replaced my old helmets with them should speak for itself.
For someone who rides as much as I do, that’s probably the strongest endorsement I can give them.
Between solid helmets like these and safe riding clothing , it’s good to feel protected!

VIENNA — Russian cargo ships have carried military equipment including tanks, armored vehicles and rocket launchers to African ports serving as gateways to Moscow’s forces on the continent, according to a new investigation that also identifies a possible additional supply route through the Republic of Congo.
The data collected by C4ADS, a Washington-based organization that tracks illicit networks globally, spans the past three years and includes a sample of a dozen ships with operational ties to Russian military shipments. The analysts used open-source information including AIS ship transponder data, satellite imagery, on-the-ground pictures and local reporting to track the ships’ journeys between 2023 and 2026.
The ports of Conakry, in Guinea; Tobruk, in Libya; and Lomé in Togo were particularly important for Russian logistics likely in support of Moscow’s Africa Corps troops. The Corps, which is under Russia’s Defense Ministry, grew out of the former Wagner Group, a paramilitary force that operated across Africa and beyond on behalf of the Kremlin’s great power politics. Mali, which C4ADS researchers suggest may have been the ultimate destination for many of the weapons shipped, is a particular Africa Corps hot spot.
The analysts tracked five known military-affiliated transport ships going from Russian Baltic and Arctic ports to Conakry between December 2024 and March 2026, from where military convoys then continued inland to Mali.
Among the ships calling at Conakry were the Adler and Siyanie Severa, which arrived in January 2025. “Within days, a convoy of roughly a hundred military vehicles, including Spartak mine-resistant ambush protected (MRAP) armored vehicles and T-72 heavy tanks, was filmed arriving in
Bamako,” the capital of Mali, C4ADS said in a write-up shared with Defense News ahead of the investigation’s publication.
Similar voyages were observed by other ships at later dates, including the Baltic Leader and Patria, which arrived in Conakry in May of the same year, after which more MRAPs appeared in the region. The pair of ships was accompanied by a third, the Siyanie Severa, which continued past Conakry to Bata, Equatorial Guinea and Lagos, Nigeria.
An attendee holds a weapon as Russian military personnel stationed in Equatorial Guinea take part in demonstrations to mark the 80th anniversary of victory over Nazi Germany, in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, on May 9, 2025. (AFP via Getty Images)
Some of the cargo ships to Africa are escorted by Russian navy ships for part or all of their voyages, such as the Sabetta, which arrived in Conakry in March 2026 after being escorted by a warship through the English Channel. C4ADS said the ship likely delivered military equipment, including Tigr infantry mobility vehicles, to Africa on that trip.
In addition to known Russian arms shipment routes, the researchers specialized on illicit network detection said that the port of Pointe-Noire in the Republic of Congo may have emerged as a new logistics hub for Russia’s military operations in Africa.
The American analysts identified three U.S.-sanctioned ships designed specifically for vehicle transport traveling from the Black Sea and St. Petersburg areas to Congo between 2023 and 2026, two of which also made voyages to West African ports that are more firmly known to be affiliated with Russian weapons shipments in the same timeframe. The researchers noted that more work was needed to conclusively determine the nature of shipments to Pointe-Noire.
Meanwhile, Libya featured as a regular destination; Russia’s Africa Corps is reportedly heavily involved in the eastern half of the country, a region that is controlled by General Haftar’s Libyan National Army.
“Like shipments to West Africa, deliveries to Libya follow a recurring pattern: departure from Baltiysk Naval Base in Kaliningrad, a naval escort indicating high-value cargo, and
frequent prolonged AIS signal gaps in the Mediterranean,” C4ADS said, calling out a tracking obfuscation technique that is also frequently used by Russia’s shadow fleet of tankers.
With regard to Togo, analysts assessed that the country had become a significant waypoint for Russian supply routes into the Sahel following a 2025 military cooperation agreement signed between Moscow and Lomé. Ships docking at the port were assessed as delivering war materiel to Mali by way of Togo and Burkina Faso.
The researchers said the cargo ship Mikhail Britnev likely carried military vehicles and equipment to Lomé in June and July 2026. Malian state television subsequently showed a convoy of 29 armored vehicles in Bamako that reporters said had traveled from Lomé.
Russian involvement in Africa is not new, dating back to the Soviet era and reinvigorated by the Wagner Group in the 2010s. The maritime routes complement an air logistics network previously investigated by Defense News , with Russian military-affiliated cargo aircraft operating through Algeria and onward to other African destinations.
C4ADS says that ten of the twelve vessels it tracked are U.S.-sanctioned, compared with six covered directly or through their owners by British sanctions and five by European Union sanctions.
The report, including an interactive map , will be released to the public on Nov. 10.

Genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000.
Genesis GV90 prices and driving range in Korea
Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.
After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August ( which we had the pleasure to see firsthand ), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.
The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.
In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.
Genesis GV90 Neolun (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).
Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis said the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).
Genesis GV90 Neolun (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
A luxury private lounge on wheels
The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.
When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”
The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.
The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.
Together, they create what Genesis calls a new realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.
Genesis GV90 Neolun infotainment display (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.
Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.
A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.
In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that shows the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.
The GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.
Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.
Genesis GV90 debut (Source: Peter Johnson/ Electrek)
Dimensions, battery size, other specs
As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.
That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).
To power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a big battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis said provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.
The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.
It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.
When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.
Genesis GV90 Neolun (left) GV90 Neolun First Edition (middle) and GV90 (right) Source: Hyundai
“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”
Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.
Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.
What do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

By Gavin van Marle
10 November 2026
Freight rates from Asia to Gulf economies trapped behind the straits of Hormuz hit unprecedented highs during this year’s peak season as importers rushed to get cargo into the region, prompting another wave of port congestion.
According to new data from Container Trades Statistics (CTS), prices on its Far East-Middle East & Indian subcontinent corridor showed the highest growth in freight rates of any major lane in container shipping so far this year.
“It’ll be no surprise that the big price index increase is Asia to India and the Middle East, where the index is up 250% since the beginning of the year and 25% month-on-month – so September’s seen a resurgence of the price there and we’re seeing some very strong prices,” CTS chief executive Nigel Pusey tells The Loadstar’s podcast today.
The last pricing data came after volumes on the route rebounded during September for the first time since the onset of conflict in the region.
“From Greater China to the Middle East, September was a bit of a boom month of volumes – China to Middle East was actually above this time last year for the first time since January and February.
“I suspect that will fall back, but what has just kept forcing its way through to the top is the price they’re paying to achieve it. We are now at a price index from Greater China to Middle East of 392, which is up 250% on the beginning of the year.
Source: Container Trades Statistics
“We have a month-on-month increase of 15.5%, despite the fact that year-to-date volumes are down 12%.
“So, at the moment, what we’ve seen is a surge of cargo in late August, early September with prices to match, although I think that will drop off in October because the attacks did come back in that early part of the month.
Source: Container Trades Statistics
According to the latest spot rate data as per the Shanghai Containerised Freight index (SCFI), freight rates appear to have hit a ceiling of $6,500 per 40ft on the SCFI’s Shanghai-Dubai leg and held at that level throughout October.
However, that is some 300% up on the $1,630 per 40ft recorded at the end of October 2025.
Meanwhile, the September surge has created some port congestion in the region, particularly at the two main ports immediately outside Hormuz – Fujairah and Khor Fakkan – which have acted as the chief landbridge gateways for GCC importers.
Linerlytica reported last week that MSC had included a call at Khor Fakkan on a new Far East-Middle East service deploying 24,000 teu ships, “despite severe berthing delays”.
“Port congestion at Middle East ports has surged to a record high,” Linerlytica added, and Mr Pusey said he expected to see liner networks flex to cope with the congestion.
“I think there’ll be some deviations. I’ve noticed one or two lines have stopped even serving cargo into Khor Fakkan and the Fujairah, which suggests that the place is getting very congested because people are trying to rush cargo through,” he told The Loadstar.
“They’re now saying, ‘Well, we’re going to stop bookings whilst we just take a bit of a breather’, and I don’t usually use my crystal ball too much, but I’m pretty sure that’s what’s going to happen in October and early November.”
In general, the use of Khor Fakkan over Fujairah has divided the liner industry into two broad camps – with MSC and the Gemini partners Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd opting for the former, while CMA CGM and its Ocean Alliance partners have their services concentrated in Fujairah, with both ports hosting increasing numbers of smaller Asian and Middle East regional carriers’ services.
Meanwhile, Maersk said shippers were returning to using the Saudi Red Sea port of Jeddah as an alternative gateway to Gulf destinations.
“Use of the Saudi Landbridge increased during October as evolving conditions at Khor Fakkan and disruption linked to the Strait of Hormuz led customers to explore alternative routings into Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf,” a Maersk statement said.
“Interest is expected to continue into November, particularly when customers are seeking to reduce exposure to disruptions affecting port and shipping connections” it added.
“The trend also highlights the value of coordinating ocean and landside planning across customer’s chosen service providers.
“However, capacity, border processing and onward delivery requirements should be confirmed for each shipment before routing decisions are finalized.”

Kearney and the MIT Mobility Initiative project that autonomous trucks will match the per-mile cost of trucks with drivers in the US around 2028, according to a report released Nov. 5 . Their model puts a driverless truck at $4 a mile in 2026, against $2.50 for a conventional truck, with the two crossing at roughly $2.60 in 2028.
The forecast adds a date to the cost case for long-haul fleets, where about half of a US truck’s cost per mile goes to the driver, according to the report. Commercial deployment is still narrow and geographically concentrated, the authors write, though Aurora’s trucks have logged more than 500,000 driverless miles on public roads.
The US crosses first, two years before Europe and four before the Middle East, because its drivers cost the most. A fully loaded US long-haul driver, including roughly 30% in benefits, costs about $10,000 a month, about twice the European cost and four times the Middle East cost, the report says.
How the forecast compares with other estimates
The conventional side of the cost comparison starts near current rates. ATRI’s Analysis of the Operational Costs of Trucking: 2026 Update put the industry-average cost to run a truck at a record $2.336 per mile in 2025, up 3.4% from 2024, a figure FreightWaves used to explain why rates are rising without more freight . Kearney’s model starts at $2.50 a mile for 2026 and rises with inflation to $3.50 by 2035.
The model assumes a $200,000 Class 8 truck with a five-year useful life, running 185,000 miles a year with two drivers who each cover 92,500 miles. Its $4-a-mile driverless cost for 2026 sits well above what some developers have published. Aurora’s own Fort Worth-to-Phoenix case study put its virtual driver cost at $1.84 a mile, against $1.99 for a human driver.
Goldman Sachs Research reached the same crossover year from a much higher starting cost. In an April 30 analysis , analyst Mark Delaney projected that autonomous trucks would become cost-competitive with human-driven trucks in the US in 2028. Goldman put the all-in autonomous cost, excluding corporate operating expenses, at about $8.56 a mile in 2025, falling to about $2.03 by 2035.
The authors built the Kearney model from more than 25 interviews with autonomous vehicle developers, truck makers, carriers, brokers, and investors.
Fleet size sets the timing
Kearney projects the driverless cost will fall to about $2 a mile by 2035, a 49% decline. Most of that drop comes from spreading the cost of building the virtual driver across more trucks. The model amortizes $750 million a year in global R&D spending over five years and assumes the fleet reaches 40,000 trucks by 2035, while remote operators go from one per 10 trucks to one per 20.
The 2028 date depends on that fleet size. If autonomous fleets reach only 10,000 trucks by 2035, US parity could slip to as late as 2032, the report says.
Regulation and liability are also unsettled. Texas, Arizona, Florida, and Georgia permit fully driverless operation, according to the report, while cross-border and many interstate routes still require a human, with no answer yet on how to certify a virtual driver. The authors also leave open how claims get split among the carrier, the truck maker, and the virtual-driver provider after an incident.
Four business models for driverless trucks
The report sorts the market into four business models: an OEM-led platform such as Volvo’s VNL Autonomous, a purpose-built vehicle such as Humble’s, an autonomous carrier such as Bot Auto, and a virtual-driver-only model such as Waabi and Aurora. The value pool all four chase is the human driver, which the report prices at $1.26 a mile.
Private truckload fleets are one of three priority segments the report names, a market of about $450 billion with an estimated $180 billion in driver costs. For-hire truckload and LTL are the other two.
“What remains to be seen is which business model captures the most value when the economics close and which players build the ecosystem position to collect it,” the authors write.
Why it matters: As AI in the physical world continues to improve, autonomous trucks and their virtual drivers are gaining greater attention from fleets and the consulting and management firms that help them make decisions. With a cost parity estimated around 2028 this supports recent bullish news from OEMs and AV developers who hope to have commercialization in place to capture that projected demand.
